lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: The instrument that is most suitable for measuring the thickness of a few sheets of cardboard is a:

(a) metre rule (b) measuring tape (c) Vernier Callipers (d) micrometer screw gauge
Correct answer: micrometer screw gauge

Q: One femtometre is equal to:

(a) 10^-9 m (b) 10^-15 m (c) 10^9 m (d) 10^15 m
Correct answer: 10^-15 m Femto stands for 10^-15, as in 5 fs = 5 x 10^-15 s given in this chapter.

Q: A light year is a unit of:

(a) light (b) time (c) distance (d) speed
Correct answer: distance One light year is calculated in this chapter as 9.46 x 10^15 m.

Q: Which one is a non-physical quantity?

(a) distance (b) density (c) colour (d) temperature
Correct answer: colour

Q: When using a measuring cylinder, one precaution to take is to:

(a) check for the zero error (b) look at the meniscus from below the level of the water surface (c) take several readings by looking from more than one direction (d) position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus
Correct answer: position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus

Q: Volume of water consumed by you per day is estimated in:

(a) millilitre (b) litre (c) kilogram (d) cubic metre
Correct answer: litre

Q: A displacement can is used to measure:

(a) mass of a liquid (b) mass of a solid (c) volume of a liquid (d) volume of a solid
Correct answer: volume of a solid

Q: Two rods with lengths 12.321 cm and 10.3 cm are placed side by side, the difference in their lengths is:

(a) 2.02 cm (b) 2.0 cm (c) 2 cm (d) 2.021 cm
Correct answer: 2.0 cm The raw difference 2.021 cm is rounded to one decimal place because 10.3 cm, the least precise measurement, has only one decimal place.

Q: Four students measure the diameter of a cylinder with Vernier Callipers. Which of the following readings is correct?

(a) 3.4 cm (b) 3.475 cm (c) 3.47 cm (d) 3.5 cm
Correct answer: 3.47 cm Vernier Callipers have a least count of 0.01 cm, so a reading must end at the second decimal place.

Q: Which of the following measures are likely to represent the thickness of a sheet of this book?

(a) 6 x 10^-25 m (b) 1 x 10^-4 m (c) 1.2 x 10^-15 m (d) 4 x 10^-2 m
Correct answer: 1 x 10^-4 m

Q: In a Vernier Callipers ten smallest divisions of the Vernier scale are equal to nine smallest divisions of the main scale. If the smallest division of the main scale is half millimetre, the Vernier constant is equal to:

(a) 0.5 mm (b) 0.1 mm (c) 0.05 mm (d) 0.001 mm
Correct answer: 0.05 mm Vernier constant = smallest main scale division divided by 10 = 0.5 mm / 10 = 0.05 mm.

Q: Note: Why is the difference 2.0 cm and not 2.021 cm?

The raw subtraction gives 12.321 - 10.3 = 2.021 cm. But a result can be no more precise than the least precise measurement used in it, and 10.3 cm is known to only one decimal place. So the answer is rounded to one decimal place: 2.0 cm.

Q: Note: Why is 3.47 cm the only possible Vernier reading?

The least count of Vernier Callipers is 0.01 cm, so every reading must be an exact multiple of 0.01 cm, i.e. it must end at the second decimal place. 3.475 cm claims a third decimal place the instrument cannot give, while 3.4 cm and 3.5 cm are metre-rule readings. Only 3.47 cm fits the instrument.

mcqs.why: A micrometer screw gauge has the smallest least count, 0.01 mm, so it can measure the very small thickness of a few sheets of cardboard accurately, unlike a metre rule or measuring tape.

mcqs.why: Femto is the prefix for 10^-15, as shown by 5 fs = 5 x 10^-15 s in the chapter, so one femtometre equals 10^-15 m.

mcqs.why: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, calculated in the chapter as 9.46 x 10^15 m, so it is a unit of distance, not of time or speed.

mcqs.why: Colour has no standard unit and cannot be measured with an instrument in the way distance, density and temperature can, so it is the non-physical quantity among the options.

options: look at the meniscus from below the level of the water surface
take several readings by looking from more than one direction
position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus
mcqs.why: Parallax and meniscus errors are avoided by positioning the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus, which is the precaution stated for measuring cylinder readings.

mcqs.why: Daily water use is a few litres, so the litre gives a convenient number; a millilitre would give a very large number and a cubic metre a very small one.

mcqs.q: A displacement can is used to measure:
mcqs.why: A displacement can collects the water displaced by a solid placed in it, and the volume of that displaced water equals the volume of the solid.

mcqs.why: Vernier Callipers have least count 0.01 cm, so a reading must end at the second decimal place; only 3.47 cm fits, while 3.475 cm claims a third decimal place the instrument cannot give.

mcqs.why: A single sheet is about a tenth of a millimetre thick, and 1 x 10^-4 m = 0.1 mm, which matches the thickness of a sheet of this book.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1.1 Can a non-physical quantity be measured? If yes, then how?

No. A non-physical quantity such as love, beauty, fear or wisdom cannot be measured with any instrument, because it has no standard unit and depends on the perception of the observer. It can only be described or estimated qualitatively, never measured exactly.

Q: 1.2 What is measurement? Name its two parts.

Measurement is the comparison of an unknown physical quantity with a known standard quantity of the same kind. Its two parts are: (1) a number, which tells how many times the standard unit is contained in the quantity, and (2) the unit itself, e.g. in 5 m, 5 is the number and metre is the unit.

Q: 1.3 Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?

A standard unit does not vary from person to person or from place to place, so a measurement made anywhere is understood in the same way everywhere. Without a standard, the same quantity would give different values for different people and fair dealing and scientific work would become impossible.

Q: 1.4 Write the name of 3 base quantities and 3 derived quantities.

Base quantities: length, mass and time (temperature, electric current, luminous intensity and amount of substance are the other four). Derived quantities: area, volume and speed (density, force and pressure are other examples), because each of them is defined in terms of base quantities.

Q: 1.5 Which SI unit will you use to express the height of your desk?

The metre (m), the SI unit of length. A desk is about 0.7 to 0.8 m high; for convenience the same height may be stated in centimetres, but the SI unit is the metre.

Q: 1.6 Write the name and symbols of all SI base units.

Length - metre (m); mass - kilogram (kg); time - second (s); temperature - kelvin (K); electric current - ampere (A); luminous intensity - candela (cd); amount of substance - mole (mol). These are the seven SI base units.

Q: 1.7 Why prefix is used? Name three sub-multiple and three multiple prefixes with their symbols.

Prefixes are used to express very large and very small quantities conveniently as multiples and sub-multiples of the SI units, so that long strings of zeros are avoided. Sub-multiples: centi (c) = 10^-2, milli (m) = 10^-3, micro = 10^-6. Multiples: kilo (k) = 10^3, mega (M) = 10^6, giga (G) = 10^9.

Q: 1.8 What is meant by: (a) 5 pm (b) 15 ns (c) 6 micrometres (d) 5 fs

(a) 5 pm = 5 picometres = 5 x 10^-12 m. (b) 15 ns = 15 nanoseconds = 15 x 10^-9 s. (c) 6 micrometres = 6 x 10^-6 m. (d) 5 fs = 5 femtoseconds = 5 x 10^-15 s. In each case the prefix fixes the power of ten by which the unit is multiplied.

Q: 1.9 (a) For what purpose, a Vernier Callipers is used? (b) Name its two main parts. (c) How is least count found? (d) What is meant by zero error?

(a) It is used to measure small lengths, external and internal diameters and depths, correctly up to 0.1 mm. (b) Its two main parts are the main scale and the sliding Vernier scale (with upper and lower jaws and a depth rod). (c) Least count = value of the smallest main scale division / number of divisions on the Vernier scale = 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm. (d) Zero error is the error when the jaws are fully closed but the zero of the Vernier scale does not coincide with the zero of the main scale; it must be added to or subtracted from every reading.

Q: 1.10 State least count and Vernier scale reading as shown in the figure and hence, find the length.

Step 1: Least count = 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm. Step 2: In the figure the zero of the Vernier scale lies just after the 2.5 cm mark, so the main scale reading is 2.5 cm. Step 3: The 5th division of the Vernier scale coincides exactly with a main scale division (the 3.0 cm line), so the Vernier reading is 5 x 0.01 cm = 0.05 cm. Step 4: Length = main scale reading + Vernier reading = 2.5 + 0.05 = 2.55 cm.

Q: 1.11 Which reading out of A, B and C shows the correct length and why?

Reading B (6.0 cm) is correct. The eye must be placed vertically above the mark to be read; at B the line of sight is perpendicular to the scale. From A and C the eye views the mark at a slant, so parallax error shifts the apparent reading to 5.9 cm and 6.1 cm.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1.1 In what unit will you express each of the following? (a) Thickness of a five-rupee coin (b) Length of a book (c) Length of football field (d) The distance between two cities (e) Mass of five-rupee coin (f) Mass of your school bag (g) Duration of your class period (h) Volume of petrol filled in the tank of a car (i) Time to boil one litre milk

(a) millimetre (mm). (b) centimetre (cm). (c) metre (m). (d) kilometre (km). (e) gram (g). (f) kilogram (kg). (g) minute (min). (h) litre (L). (i) minute (min). In each case the unit is chosen so that the measured number is of a convenient size.

Q: 1.2 Why might a standard system of measurement be helpful to a tailor?

A tailor measures cloth and body sizes for customers who may order from another city or country. With a standard system (metre, centimetre), the size he records is exactly the size understood everywhere, so garments fit correctly, cloth is bought in the right quantity, and there is no dispute caused by local units of different sizes.

Q: 1.3 The minimum main scale reading of a micrometer screw gauge is 1 mm and there are 100 divisions on the circular scale. When thimble is rotated once, 1 mm is its measurement on the main scale. What is the least count of the instrument? The reading for thickness of a steel rod as shown in the figure. What is the thickness of the rod?

Step 1: Least count = pitch / number of circular scale divisions = 1 mm / 100 = 0.01 mm. Step 2: In the figure the main scale reading is 5 mm (the last whole millimetre mark exposed before the thimble). Step 3: The 70th division of the circular scale coincides with the datum line, so the circular scale reading is 70 x 0.01 mm = 0.70 mm. Step 4: Thickness of the rod = 5 mm + 0.70 mm = 5.70 mm.

Q: 1.4 You are provided a metre scale and a bundle of pencils; how can the diameter of a pencil be measured using the metre scale with the same precision as that of Vernier Callipers? Describe briefly.

Place a number of pencils (say 10 or 20) side by side, tightly packed with no gaps, between two blocks on the metre scale and measure the total width occupied by all of them. Then divide the total width by the number of pencils. Because the total width is large, the metre scale measures it accurately, and dividing shares that accuracy among the pencils, giving each diameter to about 0.1 mm, the precision of Vernier Callipers.

Q: 1.5 The end of a metre scale is worn out. Where will you place a pencil to find the length?

Do not start from the worn zero end. Place one end of the pencil at some clear full mark, e.g. the 1 cm line, and read the scale at the other end of the pencil. The length is the difference of the two readings: final reading minus 1 cm.

Q: 1.6 Why is it better to place the object close to the metre scale?

If there is a gap between the object and the scale, the ends of the object are viewed at a slant from any normal eye position, and parallax makes the readings shift. Placing the object touching the scale removes this parallax error, so the length is read correctly.

Q: 1.7 Why a standard unit is needed to measure a quantity correctly?

A measurement is a comparison with a unit; if the unit is not standard, it differs from person to person and the comparison is meaningless. A standard unit is fixed, accepted by everyone and reproducible anywhere, so the quantity is measured correctly and the result can be repeated and trusted by all.

Q: 1.8 Suggest some natural phenomena that could serve as a reasonably accurate time standard.

The rotation of the Earth on its axis (one solar day), the revolution of the Earth around the Sun (one year), the phases of the Moon (one lunar month), the regular swing of a pendulum, and the vibrations of atoms such as caesium, which are so regular that the modern second is defined by them.

Q: 1.9 It is difficult to locate the meniscus in a wider vessel. Why?

In a wide vessel the liquid surface is almost flat: the curved meniscus forms only near the walls and the level changes very little even for a large change of volume. So the exact bottom of the meniscus cannot be located precisely, and volume readings become uncertain.

Q: 1.10 Which instrument can be used to measure: (i) internal diameter of a test tube (ii) depth of a beaker?

Vernier Callipers in both cases. (i) Its upper (inside) jaws are inserted into the test tube to read the internal diameter. (ii) Its depth rod slides out from the end of the main scale and is lowered to the bottom of the beaker to read the depth.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1.1 What is meant by base and derived quantities? Give the names and symbols of SI base units.

Base quantities are the seven independent quantities in terms of which all other quantities are defined: length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, luminous intensity and amount of substance. Their SI units are: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K), ampere (A), candela (cd) and mole (mol). Derived quantities are those defined by combining base quantities, e.g. speed = length / time, area = length x length, force = mass x length / time^2; their units, built from the base units, are called derived units.

Q: 1.2 Give three examples of derived unit in SI. How are they derived from base units? Describe briefly.

(1) Area: length x length, so its unit is m x m = m^2. (2) Speed: distance / time, so its unit is m / s = m s^-1. (3) Density: mass / volume = mass / (length)^3, so its unit is kg / m^3 = kg m^-3. In each case the derived unit is obtained by applying the same multiplication or division to the base units as the defining relation applies to the quantities.

Q: 1.3 State the similarities and differences between Vernier Callipers and micrometer screw gauge.

Similarities: both measure small lengths accurately, both have a main scale, and both need a zero-error check before use. Differences: (1) Least count of Vernier Callipers is 0.1 mm, of the screw gauge 0.01 mm, so the screw gauge is ten times more precise. (2) Vernier Callipers measure internal and external diameters and depths with jaws and a depth rod; the screw gauge measures only the thickness or diameter of small objects such as a wire or a sheet between its spindle and anvil. (3) The screw gauge works on the rotation of a thimble over a circular scale, the Callipers on a sliding Vernier scale.

Q: 1.4 Identity and explain the reasons for human errors, random errors and systematic errors in experiments.

Human errors come from the observer: carelessness, reading the scale from a slant (parallax), or mishandling the instrument. Random errors are unpredictable small fluctuations, e.g. changes in temperature or voltage, or slightly different judgements of the same reading; they make repeated readings scatter on both sides of the true value and are reduced by taking averages. Systematic errors act in one direction only and come from the instrument or method: zero error of a scale, a faulty or wrongly calibrated instrument, or a worn-out end; they shift every reading by the same amount and are removed by correcting the instrument or the method.

Q: 1.5 Differentiate between precision and accuracy of a measurement with examples.

Precision tells how finely a measurement is made; it is decided by the least count of the instrument. A screw gauge (0.01 mm) gives a more precise length than Vernier Callipers (0.1 mm). Accuracy tells how close the measured value is to the true value; it depends on the correctness of the instrument and the method. Example: a watch may read time to the nearest second (precise) yet run five minutes fast (inaccurate); another watch showing only hours may still show the correct hour (accurate but not precise).

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1.1 Calculate the number of seconds in a (a) day (b) week (c) month and state your answers using SI prefixes.

Given: 1 day = 24 h, 1 h = 60 min, 1 min = 60 s. Step 1: Seconds in one hour = 60 x 60 = 3600 s. Step 2: (a) Day = 24 x 3600 s = 86400 s = 86.4 x 10^3 s = 86.4 ks. Step 3: (b) Week = 7 x 86400 s = 604800 s = 604.8 x 10^3 s = 604.8 ks. Step 4: (c) Month of 30 days = 30 x 86400 s = 2592000 s = 2.592 x 10^6 s = 2.592 Ms.

Q: 1.2 State the answers of problem 1.1 in scientific notation.

Step 1: 86400 s = 8.64 x 10^4 s. Step 2: 604800 s = 6.048 x 10^5 s. Step 3: 2592000 s = 2.592 x 10^6 s. In scientific notation the number is written with one non-zero digit before the decimal point, multiplied by a power of ten.

Q: 1.3 Solve the following addition or subtraction. State your answers in scientific notation. (a) 4 x 10^-4 kg + 3 x 10^-5 kg (b) 5.4 x 10^-6 m - 3.2 x 10^-5 m

Rule: first make the powers of ten equal. (a) Step 1: 3 x 10^-5 kg = 0.3 x 10^-4 kg. Step 2: 4 x 10^-4 + 0.3 x 10^-4 = 4.3 x 10^-4 kg. (b) Step 1: 5.4 x 10^-6 m = 0.54 x 10^-5 m. Step 2: 0.54 x 10^-5 - 3.2 x 10^-5 = -2.66 x 10^-5 m.

Q: 1.4 Solve the following multiplication or division. State your answers in scientific notation. (a) (5 x 10^4 m) x (3 x 10^-2 m) (b) (6 x 10^8 kg) / (3 x 10^4 m^3)

Rule: multiply or divide the numbers, and add or subtract the powers of ten. (a) Step 1: 5 x 3 = 15. Step 2: 10^4 x 10^-2 = 10^2. Step 3: Result = 15 x 10^2 = 1.5 x 10^3 m^2. (b) Step 1: 6 / 3 = 2.0. Step 2: 10^8 / 10^4 = 10^4. Step 3: Result = 2.0 x 10^4 kg m^-3.

Q: 1.5 Calculate the following and state your answer in scientific notation. [(3 x 10^2 kg) x (4.0 km)] / (5 x 10^2 s^2)

Step 1: Convert to SI units: 4.0 km = 4.0 x 10^3 m. Step 2: Numerator = 3 x 10^2 x 4.0 x 10^3 = 12 x 10^5 = 1.2 x 10^6 kg m. Step 3: Divide by 5 x 10^2 s^2: 1.2 x 10^6 / 5 x 10^2 = 0.24 x 10^4 = 2.4 x 10^3. Final answer: 2.4 x 10^3 kg m s^-2.

Q: 1.6 State the number of significant digits in each measurement. (a) 0.0045 m (b) 2.047 m (c) 3.40 m (d) 3.420 x 10^4 m

Rule: leading zeros are not significant; zeros between digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. (a) 0.0045 m: only 4 and 5 count = 2 significant digits. (b) 2.047 m: all four digits count = 4. (c) 3.40 m: 3, 4 and the trailing 0 count = 3. (d) 3.420 x 10^4 m: 3, 4, 2 and the trailing 0 count = 4.

Q: 1.7 Write in scientific notation: (a) 0.0035 m (b) 206.4 x 10^2 m

(a) Step 1: Move the decimal point to just after the first non-zero digit: 3.5. Step 2: The point moved 3 places to the right, so 0.0035 m = 3.5 x 10^-3 m. (b) Step 1: 206.4 = 2.064 x 10^2. Step 2: 2.064 x 10^2 x 10^2 = 2.064 x 10^4 m.

Q: 1.8 Write using correct prefixes: (a) 5.0 x 10^4 cm (b) 580 x 10^2 g (c) 45 x 10^-4 s

(a) Step 1: 5.0 x 10^4 cm = 5.0 x 10^4 x 10^-2 m = 5.0 x 10^2 m. Step 2: 5.0 x 10^2 m = 0.5 x 10^3 m = 0.5 km. (b) Step 1: 580 x 10^2 g = 58000 g = 58 x 10^3 g. Step 2: 58 x 10^3 g = 58 kg. (c) Step 1: 45 x 10^-4 s = 4.5 x 10^-3 s. Step 2: 10^-3 is milli, so the answer is 4.5 ms.

Q: 1.9 Light year is a unit of distance used in Astronomy. It is the distance covered by light in one year. Taking the speed of light as 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1, calculate the distance.

Given: speed of light c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s; time = 1 year. Step 1: Time in seconds = 365 x 24 x 60 x 60 = 3.1536 x 10^7 s, about 3.16 x 10^7 s. Step 2: Formula: distance = speed x time. Step 3: Distance = 3.0 x 10^8 x 3.1536 x 10^7 = 9.46 x 10^15 m. Final answer: 1 light year = 9.46 x 10^15 m.

Q: 1.10 Express the density of mercury given as 13.6 g cm^-3 in kg m^-3.

Given: density = 13.6 g/cm^3. Step 1: 1 g = 10^-3 kg, so 13.6 g = 13.6 x 10^-3 kg. Step 2: 1 cm^3 = (10^-2 m)^3 = 10^-6 m^3. Step 3: Density = mass / volume = 13.6 x 10^-3 kg / 10^-6 m^3 = 13.6 x 10^3 kg/m^3. Final answer: 1.36 x 10^4 kg m^-3.

mcqs.q: The number of seconds in a day is:
mcqs.why: Given: 1 day = 24 h, 1 h = 60 min, 1 min = 60 s. Seconds in one hour = 60 x 60 = 3600 s. Substitution: seconds in a day = 24 x 3600 s = 86400 s = 86.4 ks.

mcqs.q: The number of seconds in a week, in scientific notation, is:
mcqs.why: Given: 1 day = 86400 s and 1 week = 7 days. Formula: seconds in a week = 7 x seconds in a day. Substitution: 7 x 86400 s = 604800 s = 6.048 x 10^5 s.

mcqs.q: 4 x 10^-4 kg + 3 x 10^-5 kg equals:
mcqs.why: Given: 4 x 10^-4 kg and 3 x 10^-5 kg. Method: first make the powers of ten equal, 3 x 10^-5 kg = 0.3 x 10^-4 kg. Substitution: 4 x 10^-4 + 0.3 x 10^-4 = 4.3 x 10^-4 kg.

mcqs.q: (5 x 10^4 m) x (3 x 10^-2 m) equals:
mcqs.why: Given: 5 x 10^4 m and 3 x 10^-2 m. Method: multiply the numbers and add the powers of ten. Substitution: 5 x 3 = 15 and 10^4 x 10^-2 = 10^2, so result = 15 x 10^2 = 1.5 x 10^3 m^2.

mcqs.q: The number of significant digits in 3.40 m is:
mcqs.why: Given measurement: 3.40 m. Rule: zeros between digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. Counting: 3, 4 and the trailing 0 all count, so the result is 3 significant digits.

mcqs.q: 0.0035 m written in scientific notation is:
mcqs.why: Given: 0.0035 m. Method: move the decimal point to just after the first non-zero digit, giving 3.5. The point moved 3 places to the right, so 0.0035 m = 3.5 x 10^-3 m.

mcqs.q: 580 x 10^2 g written using the correct prefix is:
mcqs.why: Given: 580 x 10^2 g = 58000 g = 58 x 10^3 g. Since 10^3 g = 1 kg, substitution gives the result 58 kg.

mcqs.q: Taking the speed of light as 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, one light year is:
mcqs.why: Given: speed of light c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s and time = 1 year = 365 x 24 x 60 x 60 = 3.1536 x 10^7 s. Formula: distance = speed x time. Substitution: 3.0 x 10^8 x 3.1536 x 10^7 = 9.46 x 10^15 m.

mcqs.q: The density of mercury, 13.6 g cm^-3, expressed in kg m^-3 is:
mcqs.why: Given: density = 13.6 g/cm^3. Convert: 13.6 g = 13.6 x 10^-3 kg and 1 cm^3 = (10^-2 m)^3 = 10^-6 m^3. Formula: density = mass / volume. Substitution: 13.6 x 10^-3 / 10^-6 = 13.6 x 10^3 = 1.36 x 10^4 kg m^-3.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: The numerical ratio of displacement to distance is:

(a) always less than one (b) always equal to one (c) always greater than one (d) equal to or less than one
Correct answer: equal to or less than one Displacement is the shortest straight-line change of position and is never greater than the distance travelled, so the ratio can be equal to one or less than one.

Q: If a body does not change its position with respect to some fixed point, then it will be in a state of:

(a) rest (b) motion (c) uniform motion (d) variable motion
Correct answer: rest A body is at rest if it does not change its position with respect to a fixed point (its surroundings) with time.

Q: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower, the distance covered by it in the first second is:

(a) 5 m (b) 10 m (c) 50 m (d) 100 m
Correct answer: 5 m For a dropped body, S = (1/2) g t^2 = (1/2) x 10 x (1)^2 = 5 m in the first second.

Q: A body accelerates from rest to a velocity of 144 km h^-1 in 20 seconds. The distance covered by it is:

(a) 100 m (b) 400 m (c) 1400 m (d) 1440 m
Correct answer: 400 m 144 km/h = 40 m/s, so a = 40 / 20 = 2 m/s^2 and S = (1/2) a t^2 = (1/2) x 2 x (20)^2 = 400 m.

Q: A body is moving with constant acceleration starting from rest. It covers a distance S in 4 seconds. How much time does it take to cover one-fourth of this distance?

(a) 1 s (b) 2 s (c) 4 s (d) 16 s
Correct answer: 2 s From rest, S = (1/2) a t^2, so distance is proportional to t^2; one-fourth of the distance needs sqrt(1/4) x 4 s = 2 s.

Q: The displacement time graphs of two objects A and B are shown in the figure. Point out the true statement from the following:

(a) The velocity of A is greater than B. (b) The velocity of A is less than B. (c) The velocity of A is equal to that of B. (d) The graph gives no information in this regard.
Correct answer: The velocity of A is greater than B. The gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity, and the steeper graph of A shows the greater velocity.

Q: The area under the speed-time graph is numerically equal to:

(a) velocity (b) uniform velocity (c) acceleration (d) distance covered
Correct answer: distance covered The area under a speed-time graph equals speed x time for each strip, which is the distance covered.

Q: Gradient of the speed-time graph is equal to:

(a) speed (b) velocity (c) acceleration (d) distance covered
Correct answer: acceleration The gradient of a speed-time graph is the change of speed in unit time, which is the acceleration.

Q: Gradient of the distance-time graph is equal to the:

(a) speed (b) velocity (c) distance covered (d) acceleration
Correct answer: speed The gradient of a distance-time graph is the change of distance in unit time, which is the speed of the body.

Q: A car accelerates uniformly from 80.5 km h^-1 at t = 0 to 113 km h^-1 at t = 9 s. Which graph best describes the motion of the car? (a) v-t curve rising with increasing slope from a positive value (b) straight line from origin (c) straight line of gentle slope starting from a positive velocity (d) line falling to zero

(a) graph (a) (b) graph (b) (c) graph (c) (d) graph (d)
Correct answer: graph (c) Uniform acceleration gives a straight-line speed-time graph; the car starts from a positive velocity of 80.5 km/h, so the line starts above zero with a gentle slope.

mcqs.q: The numerical ratio of displacement to distance is:
options: equal to or less than one
mcqs.why: Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from start to finish and can never exceed the actual path length (distance), so displacement/distance is equal to or less than one.

mcqs.q: If a body does not change its position with respect to some fixed point, then it will be in a state of:
mcqs.why: By definition a body is at rest when it does not change its position with respect to some fixed point or its surroundings with time.

mcqs.q: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower, the distance covered by it in the first second is:
mcqs.why: Using h = (1/2) g t^2 with g = 10 m/s^2 and t = 1 s: h = 0.5 x 10 x 1 = 5 m, so a dropped ball covers 5 m in the first second.

mcqs.q: A body accelerates from rest to a velocity of 144 km h^-1 in 20 seconds. The distance covered by it is:
A body is moving with constant acceleration starting from rest. It covers a distance S in 4 seconds. How much time does it take to cover one-fourth of this distance?
mcqs.why: From rest S = (1/2) a t^2, so S is proportional to t^2. For S/4 the time is 4 x sqrt(1/4) = 4 x 1/2 = 2 s.

mcqs.q: The displacement time graphs of two objects A and B are shown in the figure. Point out the true statement from the following:
options: The velocity of A is greater than B.
The velocity of A is less than B.
The velocity of A is equal to that of B.
The graph gives no information in this regard.
mcqs.why: Velocity equals the gradient of a displacement-time graph. Graph A is steeper than graph B, so the velocity of A is greater than that of B.

mcqs.q: The area under the speed-time graph is numerically equal to:
mcqs.why: Area under a speed-time graph = speed x time, and speed x time is the distance covered, as proved for the uniform-speed rectangle and for thin strips when speed changes.

mcqs.q: Gradient of the speed-time graph is equal to:
mcqs.why: The gradient of a speed-time graph is the change in speed divided by the time taken, which is exactly the definition of acceleration.

mcqs.q: Gradient of the distance-time graph is equal to the:
mcqs.why: The gradient of a distance-time graph is the change in distance divided by the time taken, which gives the speed of the body, as stated in the chapter Key Points.

mcqs.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 80.5 km h^-1 at t = 0 to 113 km h^-1 at t = 9 s. Which graph best describes the motion of the car? (a) v-t curve rising with increasing slope from a positive value (b) straight line from origin (c) straight line of gentle slope starting from a positive velocity (d) line falling to zero
mcqs.why: The car accelerates uniformly, so its speed-time graph is a straight line; it starts at a positive velocity (80.5 km/h) and rises gently, which is graph (c).

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2.1 Define scalar and vector quantities.

A scalar quantity is a physical quantity which can be described completely by its magnitude only, e.g. distance, speed, mass, time and temperature. A vector quantity is a physical quantity which needs magnitude as well as direction to be described completely, e.g. displacement, velocity, acceleration, weight and force.

Q: 2.2 Give 5 examples each for scalar and vector quantities.

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, time, energy (also temperature, volume, density). Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight (also momentum). Scalars are added like ordinary numbers; vectors can only be added by rules that also account for direction.

Q: 2.3 State head-to-tail rule for addition of vectors.

To add a number of vectors, redraw their representative lines so that the head of one line coincides with the tail of the next, in the same order and direction. The resultant vector is the single line drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector; its length gives the magnitude and its direction gives the direction of the sum.

Q: 2.4 What are distance-time graph and speed-time graph?

A distance-time graph shows how the distance covered by a moving body changes with time; its gradient gives the speed of the body. A speed-time graph shows how the speed of the body changes with time; its gradient gives the acceleration, and the area under it gives the distance covered.

Q: 2.5 Falling objects near the Earth have the same constant acceleration. Does this imply that a heavier object will fall faster than a lighter object?

No. Near the Earth every freely falling object, heavy or light, has the same acceleration g (about 10 m/s^2) when air resistance is neglected. Both gain speed at the same rate and, dropped from the same height, reach the ground together. In air, a light object may appear slower only because air resistance affects it more.

Q: 2.6 The vector quantities are sometimes written in scalar notation (not bold face). How is the direction indicated?

When a vector is written in ordinary (scalar) type, an arrow is placed above its symbol, e.g. an arrow over v for velocity or over F for force. In print, vectors are often shown in bold face instead; the arrow notation carries the same meaning: the symbol stands for magnitude together with the stated direction.

Q: 2.7 A body is moving with uniform speed. Will its velocity be uniform? Give reason.

Not necessarily. Velocity is uniform only if both speed and direction remain unchanged. A body moving with uniform speed in a circle (e.g. a car going round a roundabout at steady speed) continually changes direction, so its velocity keeps changing and is not uniform. Only if it moves in a straight line at uniform speed is its velocity uniform.

Q: 2.8 Is it possible for a body to have acceleration? When moving with: (i) constant velocity (ii) constant speed

(i) No. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; with constant velocity there is no change, so acceleration is zero. (ii) Yes. With constant speed the direction may still change, as in circular motion; velocity then changes and the body has acceleration (towards the centre of the circle).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
mcqs.why: A scalar is described completely by magnitude only. Distance has magnitude only, while displacement, velocity and force also need a direction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
mcqs.why: Velocity needs magnitude as well as direction to be described completely, so it is a vector; speed, mass and time are scalars with magnitude only.

mcqs.q: In the head-to-tail rule, the resultant vector is drawn from:
options: The head of the first vector to the tail of the last vector
The tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector
The head of one vector to the head of the next
The tail of the last vector to the tail of the first vector
mcqs.why: After joining the vectors head-to-tail in the same order and direction, the single line from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector is the resultant; its length gives the magnitude and its direction gives the direction of the sum.

mcqs.q: The gradient of a distance-time graph gives:
mcqs.why: A distance-time graph shows how distance changes with time, and its gradient (change in distance / time) gives the speed of the body.

mcqs.q: The area under a speed-time graph gives:
mcqs.why: A speed-time graph shows how speed changes with time; the area under it gives the distance covered, while its gradient gives the acceleration.

mcqs.q: The gradient of a speed-time graph gives:
mcqs.why: The gradient of a speed-time graph is the change of speed in unit time, which is the acceleration of the body.

mcqs.q: A heavier object and a lighter object are dropped from the same height near the Earth (air resistance neglected). Which falls faster?
options: Neither; both have the same acceleration g and reach the ground together
The one with the larger size
mcqs.why: Near the Earth every freely falling object, heavy or light, has the same acceleration g (about 10 m/s^2) when air resistance is neglected, so both gain speed at the same rate and reach the ground together.

mcqs.q: When a vector is written in ordinary (scalar) type, its direction is indicated by:
options: Placing an arrow above its symbol
Adding a degree sign after it
mcqs.why: In ordinary type an arrow is placed above the symbol, e.g. an arrow over v for velocity or over F for force; in print, bold face is often used instead with the same meaning.

mcqs.q: A car goes round a roundabout at uniform (steady) speed. Its velocity is:
options: Uniform, because its speed is steady
Zero, because it returns to the start
Not uniform, because its direction continually changes
Equal to its speed in every direction
mcqs.why: Velocity is uniform only if both speed and direction remain unchanged. In circular motion the direction keeps changing, so the velocity keeps changing and is not uniform.

mcqs.q: Which statement about acceleration is correct?
options: With constant velocity, acceleration is zero; with constant speed, acceleration is possible if the direction changes
With constant velocity, acceleration can be non-zero
With constant speed, acceleration is always zero
Acceleration exists only when speed increases
mcqs.why: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. With constant velocity there is no change, so acceleration is zero; with constant speed the direction may still change, as in circular motion, so the body can have acceleration towards the centre of the circle.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2.1 Distance and displacement may or may not be equal in magnitude. Explain this statement.

Distance is the total length of the path followed; displacement is the straight-line change of position from start to finish. For motion along a straight line in one direction the path length equals the straight-line change, so the two are equal. For any curved path, or motion that reverses, the path is longer than the straight-line change, so distance is greater than the magnitude of displacement; for a complete round trip the displacement is zero while the distance is the whole path length.

Q: 2.2 When a bullet is fired, its velocity with which it leaves the barrel is called the muzzle velocity of the gun. The muzzle velocity of one gun with a longer barrel is lesser than that of another gun with a shorter barrel. In which gun is the acceleration of the bullet larger? Explain your answer.

In the gun with the shorter barrel. The bullet starts from rest in both guns. Acceleration is judged with the distance available: from 2aS = vf^2 - vi^2, a = vf^2 / 2S (vi = 0). The shorter-barrel gun gives a larger final velocity vf in a smaller distance S, so both effects make its acceleration larger: the propelling force speeds the bullet up more strongly over the shorter travel.

Q: 2.3 For a complete trip, average velocity was calculated. Its value came out to be positive. Is it possible that its instantaneous velocity at any time during the trip had the negative value? Give justification of your answer.

Yes, it is possible. Average velocity depends only on the total displacement and total time; a positive value means the final position is on the positive side of the start. During the trip the body may move backwards for a while (negative instantaneous velocity), e.g. overshooting a point and returning, yet still finish with a net positive displacement, so the average stays positive.

Q: 2.4 A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity v. It returns to the ground in time T. Which of the following graphs correctly represents the motion? Explain your reasoning. (a) v-t V-shaped graph touching zero at T/2 (b) two straight branches crossing at T/2 (c) straight line from +v through zero at T/2 to a negative value at T (d) triangular graph from zero up and back to zero at T

Graph (c) is correct. Taking upward as positive, the velocity starts at +v and decreases uniformly under gravity: v(t) = v - gt, a straight line of slope -g. It becomes zero at the top, at t = T/2, then negative as the ball falls, reaching -v at t = T. Graph (a) plots speed, not velocity (speed is never negative and rises again after T/2); graph (d) wrongly starts from zero velocity; graph (b) shows two motions at once.

Q: 2.5 The figure given below shows the distance-time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c. (Graph: distance rises to 2.0 km at 6 min, stays level until 10 min, then falls to zero at 20 min.)

Velocity = gradient of the distance-time graph = change in distance / time taken. Step 1: Segment a: distance rises from 0 to 2.0 km in 6 min, so v = 2.0 km / 6 min = 0.333 km/min = 20 km/h (moving away). Step 2: Segment b: distance stays 2.0 km from 6 to 10 min, gradient is zero, so v = 0; the cyclist is at rest. Step 3: Segment c: distance falls from 2.0 km to 0 in 10 min (10 to 20 min), so v = -2.0 km / 10 min = -0.2 km/min = -12 km/h; the negative sign shows he is returning towards the start at 12 km/h.

Q: 2.6 Is it possible that the velocity of an object is zero at an instant of time, but its acceleration is not zero? If yes, give an example of such a case.

Yes. A ball thrown vertically upwards has zero velocity at the highest point of its flight, but gravity still acts on it, so its acceleration is g = 10 m/s^2 downwards at that instant too. That is why it does not stay at the top but starts falling back.

mcqs.q: Distance and the magnitude of displacement are equal when a body moves:
options: Along a straight line in one direction
Back and forth on a line
mcqs.why: For motion along a straight line in one direction, the path length equals the straight-line change of position, so distance and displacement are equal in magnitude.

mcqs.q: For a complete round trip, the displacement of a body is:
options: Equal to the whole path length
Zero, while the distance is the whole path length
mcqs.why: Displacement is the straight-line change of position from start to finish. A complete round trip ends at the start, so the displacement is zero while the distance is the whole path length.

mcqs.q: A gun with a shorter barrel gives a larger muzzle velocity in a smaller distance than a longer-barrel gun. The acceleration of its bullet is larger because, from a = vf^2 / 2S (vi = 0):
options: Both a larger vf and a smaller S make a larger
A smaller S always makes a smaller
Only the barrel length matters, not vf
The formula gives a smaller a for the shorter barrel
mcqs.why: From 2aS = vf^2 - vi^2 with vi = 0, a = vf^2 / 2S. The shorter-barrel gun gives a larger final velocity vf in a smaller distance S, so both effects make its acceleration larger.

mcqs.q: The average velocity for a complete trip is positive. Can the instantaneous velocity at some time during the trip be negative?
options: No, every instantaneous velocity must also be positive
Yes, if the body moves backwards for a while but still finishes with a net positive displacement
Only if the average velocity is zero
Only if the body stops during the trip
mcqs.why: Average velocity depends only on total displacement and total time. The body may move backwards for a while (negative instantaneous velocity), e.g. overshooting a point and returning, yet finish with a net positive displacement, so the average stays positive.

mcqs.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity v and returns to the ground in time T. Its velocity-time graph (upward taken as positive) is:
options: A V-shaped graph touching zero at T/2
A triangular graph starting from zero
Two straight branches crossing at T/2
A straight line from +v through zero at T/2 to a negative value at T
mcqs.why: Velocity decreases uniformly under gravity: v(t) = v - gt, a straight line of slope -g. It is zero at the top at t = T/2, then negative as the ball falls, reaching -v at t = T, which is graph (c).

mcqs.q: A cyclist's distance-time graph rises from 0 to 2.0 km in the first 6 min (segment a). His velocity in segment a is:
mcqs.why: Velocity = gradient of the distance-time graph = change in distance / time = 2.0 km / 6 min = 0.333 km/min = 20 km/h, moving away from the start.

mcqs.q: In segment b of the cyclist's graph, the distance stays at 2.0 km from 6 to 10 min. His velocity is:
mcqs.why: In segment b the distance does not change, so the gradient of the distance-time graph is zero and the velocity is 0; the cyclist is at rest.

mcqs.q: In segment c, the cyclist's distance falls from 2.0 km to 0 in 10 min (from 10 to 20 min). His velocity is:
mcqs.why: Velocity = -2.0 km / 10 min = -0.2 km/min = -12 km/h. The negative sign shows he is returning towards the start at 12 km/h.

mcqs.q: Can a body's velocity be zero at an instant while its acceleration is not zero?
options: No, zero velocity always means zero acceleration
Only for a body at rest on the ground
Yes; e.g. a ball thrown vertically upwards has zero velocity at its highest point but acceleration g downwards
Only if gravity is switched off
mcqs.why: A ball thrown vertically upwards has zero velocity at the highest point of its flight, but gravity still acts on it, so its acceleration is g downwards at that instant too, which is why it starts falling back.

mcqs.q: At the highest point of its flight, the acceleration of a ball thrown vertically upwards is:
mcqs.why: Gravity acts on the ball throughout its flight, so at the highest point its acceleration is g = 10 m/s^2 downwards even though its velocity is zero at that instant.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2.1 How a vector can be represented graphically? Explain.

A vector is represented graphically by a straight line with an arrowhead, drawn to a chosen scale. The length of the line is proportional to the magnitude of the vector (according to the scale), the line is drawn in the direction of the vector, and the arrowhead shows the sense of that direction. The starting point of the line is called the tail and the arrow end the head. Example: a velocity of 40 m/s towards east can be drawn as a 4 cm line pointing east with the scale 1 cm = 10 m/s.

Q: 2.2 Differentiate between: (i) rest and motion (ii) speed and velocity

(i) A body is at rest if it does not change its position with respect to a fixed point (its surroundings) with time; it is in motion if its position keeps changing with time. Rest and motion are relative to the chosen surroundings. (ii) Speed is the distance covered in unit time; it is a scalar and is always positive. Velocity is the displacement in unit time in a stated direction; it is a vector and can be positive, negative or zero. Speed = distance / time, velocity = displacement / time.

Q: 2.3 Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.

(1) Translatory motion: every part of the body moves through the same distance in the same direction; it may be linear (a car on a straight road), random (a bee flying) or circular (a car going round a curve). (2) Rotatory motion: the body spins about a fixed axis, e.g. a ceiling fan, the Earth rotating, a wheel. (3) Vibratory motion: the body moves to and fro about a mean position, e.g. a pendulum, a guitar string, a swing.

Q: 2.4 Explain the difference between distance and displacement.

Distance is the length of the actual path travelled by a body, whatever its shape; it is a scalar quantity, measured in metres, and is never negative or zero for a moving body. Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position, together with its direction; it is a vector quantity. Displacement can be equal to the distance (straight motion in one direction), smaller than it (curved or reversed path), or zero (closed trip), but never greater.

Q: 2.5 What do gradients of distance-time graph and speed-time graph represent? Explain it by drawing diagrams.

The gradient of a distance-time graph represents the speed of the body: a steep straight line means fast steady motion, a horizontal line means rest, and a curve of increasing slope means acceleration. The gradient of a speed-time graph represents the acceleration of the body: a straight line sloping up means uniform acceleration, a horizontal line means uniform speed (zero acceleration), and a line sloping down means retardation. (In the notes, draw: distance-time axes with a straight rising line labelled speed = gradient; speed-time axes with a straight rising line labelled acceleration = gradient.)

Q: 2.6 Prove that the area under speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered by an object.

Consider a body moving with uniform speed v for time t; its speed-time graph is a horizontal line at height v. Step 1: Distance covered S = speed x time = v x t. Step 2: On the graph, v is the height and t is the width, so v x t is exactly the area of the rectangle under the graph. Step 3: Hence area under the speed-time graph = distance covered. The same result holds for changing speed by dividing the area into thin strips, each giving the distance covered in its small time interval.

Q: 2.7 How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?

For bodies moving freely under gravity, the acceleration a in the equations of motion is replaced by g (10 m/s^2) and the distance S by the height h. The equations become: vf = vi + gt; h = vi t + (1/2) g t^2; 2gh = vf^2 - vi^2. For a falling body vi = 0 and g is taken positive (downward). For a body thrown upward, g acts against the motion, so it is taken negative: vf = vi - gt, and at the highest point vf = 0.

mcqs.q: How is a vector represented graphically?
options: By a curved line with a dot at the end
By a straight line with an arrowhead, drawn to a chosen scale, whose length is proportional to the magnitude and whose direction is the direction of the vector
By a circle whose radius is the magnitude
By two parallel lines showing magnitude only
mcqs.why: A vector is drawn as a straight line with an arrowhead to a chosen scale: the length is proportional to the magnitude, the line is drawn in the direction of the vector, and the arrowhead shows the sense of that direction.

mcqs.q: A velocity of 40 m/s towards east is drawn with the scale 1 cm = 10 m/s. The representative line is:
options: 4 cm long pointing east, with an arrowhead
mcqs.why: Length = magnitude / scale value = 40 / 10 = 4 cm. The line is drawn 4 cm long pointing east with an arrowhead at its end, starting at the tail and ending at the head.

mcqs.q: A body is said to be at rest if:
options: It does not change its position with respect to a fixed point (its surroundings) with time
It moves on a straight road
No force acts on it at all
mcqs.why: A body is at rest if it does not change its position with respect to a fixed point with time; it is in motion if its position keeps changing with time. Rest and motion are relative to the chosen surroundings.

mcqs.q: Velocity differs from speed because velocity is:
options: The displacement in unit time in a stated direction; it is a vector and can be positive, negative or zero
The distance in unit time with a direction added afterwards
mcqs.why: Speed = distance / time; it is a scalar and always positive. Velocity = displacement / time in a stated direction; it is a vector and can be positive, negative or zero.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of rotatory motion?
options: A bee flying from flower to flower
A pendulum swinging to and fro
A ceiling fan spinning about a fixed axis
A car moving on a straight road
mcqs.why: In rotatory motion the body spins about a fixed axis, e.g. a ceiling fan, the Earth rotating, or a wheel. A bee flying is random translatory motion and a pendulum is vibratory motion.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of vibratory motion?
options: A guitar string moving to and fro about its mean position
A wheel rolling on a road
A car going round a curve
The Earth rotating on its axis
mcqs.why: Vibratory motion is to-and-fro motion about a mean position, e.g. a pendulum, a guitar string, or a swing.

mcqs.q: Displacement, compared with the distance travelled, can be:
options: Greater than the distance for a curved path
Equal to, smaller than, or zero compared with the distance, but never greater
Always zero for a moving body
mcqs.why: Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position with direction. It equals the distance for straight motion in one direction, is smaller for a curved or reversed path, and is zero for a closed trip, but never greater.

mcqs.q: The gradient of a distance-time graph represents:
options: Speed; a steep straight line means fast steady motion and a horizontal line means rest
mcqs.why: The gradient of a distance-time graph represents the speed of the body: a steep straight line means fast steady motion, a horizontal line means rest, and a curve of increasing slope means acceleration.

mcqs.q: For a body moving with uniform speed v for time t, the area under its speed-time graph equals the distance covered because:
options: Distance S = v x t, and v (height) x t (width) is exactly the area of the rectangle under the graph
The graph is always a triangle
Area and distance have the same unit symbol
The gradient of the graph is zero
mcqs.why: Distance covered S = speed x time = v x t. On the graph v is the height and t is the width, so v x t is exactly the area of the rectangle under the graph; hence area under the speed-time graph = distance covered.

mcqs.q: For a body thrown vertically upward, the equations of motion under gravity are applied by:
options: Taking g positive because the body is moving
Taking g negative (it acts against the motion), so vf = vi - gt, and at the highest point vf = 0
Setting g = 0 at the highest point
Replacing t with h in every equation
mcqs.why: Under gravity a is replaced by g (10 m/s^2) and S by h: vf = vi + gt, h = vi t + (1/2) g t^2, 2gh = vf^2 - vi^2. For a body thrown upward g acts against the motion, so it is taken negative: vf = vi - gt, and at the highest point vf = 0.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2.1 Draw the representative lines of the following vectors: (a) A velocity of 400 m s^-1 making an angle of 60 degrees with x-axis. (b) A force of 50 N making an angle of 120 degrees with x-axis.

(a) Choose the scale 1 cm = 100 m/s. Step 1: Magnitude 400 m/s is represented by a line of 400 / 100 = 4 cm. Step 2: Draw the x-axis, and from a point on it draw a 4 cm line at 60 degrees above the axis, with an arrowhead at its end. This line represents the velocity. (b) Choose the scale 1 cm = 10 N. Step 1: Magnitude 50 N is represented by a line of 50 / 10 = 5 cm. Step 2: Draw a 5 cm line at 120 degrees from the x-axis (i.e. 60 degrees past the vertical, into the second quadrant), with an arrowhead at its end. This line represents the force.

Q: 2.2 A car is moving with an average speed of 72 km h^-1. How much time will it take to cover a distance of 360 km?

Given: average speed v = 72 km/h; distance S = 360 km. Step 1: Formula: time = distance / average speed, t = S / v. Step 2: Substitute: t = 360 km / 72 km/h. Step 3: t = 5 h. Final answer: 5 hours.

Q: 2.3 A truck starts from rest. It reaches a velocity of 90 km h^-1 in 50 seconds. Find its average acceleration.

Given: initial velocity vi = 0; final velocity vf = 90 km/h; time t = 50 s. Step 1: Convert velocity to SI units: vf = 90 x 1000 / 3600 = 25 m/s. Step 2: Formula: a = (vf - vi) / t. Step 3: Substitute: a = (25 - 0) / 50 = 0.5. Final answer: average acceleration = 0.5 m/s^2.

Q: 2.4 A car passes a green traffic signal while moving with a velocity of 5 m s^-1. It then accelerates to 1.5 m s^-2. What is the velocity of car after 5 seconds?

Given: initial velocity vi = 5 m/s; acceleration a = 1.5 m/s^2; time t = 5 s. Step 1: Formula (first equation of motion): vf = vi + a t. Step 2: Substitute: vf = 5 + 1.5 x 5 = 5 + 7.5. Step 3: vf = 12.5. Final answer: velocity after 5 s = 12.5 m/s.

Q: 2.5 A motorcycle initially travelling at 18 km h^-1 accelerates at constant rate of 2 m s^-2. How far will the motorcycle go in 10 seconds?

Given: initial velocity vi = 18 km/h; acceleration a = 2 m/s^2; time t = 10 s. Step 1: Convert velocity: vi = 18 x 1000 / 3600 = 5 m/s. Step 2: Formula (second equation of motion): S = vi t + (1/2) a t^2. Step 3: Substitute: S = 5 x 10 + (1/2) x 2 x (10)^2 = 50 + 100. Step 4: S = 150. Final answer: distance covered = 150 m.

Q: 2.6 A wagon is moving on the road with a velocity of 54 km h^-1. Brakes are applied suddenly. The wagon covers a distance of 25 m before stopping. Determine the acceleration of the wagon.

Given: initial velocity vi = 54 km/h; final velocity vf = 0; distance S = 25 m. Step 1: Convert velocity: vi = 54 x 1000 / 3600 = 15 m/s. Step 2: Formula (third equation of motion): 2 a S = vf^2 - vi^2. Step 3: Substitute: 2 x a x 25 = 0 - (15)^2 = -225. Step 4: a = -225 / 50 = -4.5. Final answer: acceleration = -4.5 m/s^2; the negative sign shows retardation of 4.5 m/s^2.

Q: 2.7 A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. How long will it take to reach the ground? What will be its velocity just before hitting the ground?

Given: height h = 45 m; initial velocity vi = 0; g = 10 m/s^2. Step 1: Formula: h = vi t + (1/2) g t^2. Step 2: Substitute: 45 = 0 + (1/2) x 10 x t^2 = 5 t^2, so t^2 = 9 and t = 3 s. Step 3: Formula: vf = vi + g t = 0 + 10 x 3 = 30 m/s. Final answer: time = 3 s; velocity on hitting the ground = 30 m/s.

Q: 2.8 A car travels 10 km with an average velocity of 20 m s^-1. Then it travels in the same direction through a diversion at an average velocity of 4 m s^-1 for the next 0.8 km. Determine the average velocity of the car for the total journey.

Given: first part S1 = 10 km = 10000 m at v1 = 20 m/s; second part S2 = 0.8 km = 800 m at v2 = 4 m/s, same direction. Step 1: Time for first part: t1 = 10000 / 20 = 500 s. Step 2: Time for second part: t2 = 800 / 4 = 200 s. Step 3: Total displacement = 10000 + 800 = 10800 m; total time = 500 + 200 = 700 s. Step 4: Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 10800 / 700 = 15.4 m/s. Final answer: 15.4 m/s.

Q: 2.9 A ball is dropped from the top of a tower. The ball reaches the ground in 5 seconds. Find the height of the tower and the velocity of the ball with which it strikes the ground.

Given: time t = 5 s; initial velocity vi = 0; g = 10 m/s^2. Step 1: Formula: h = vi t + (1/2) g t^2. Step 2: Substitute: h = 0 + (1/2) x 10 x (5)^2 = 5 x 25 = 125 m. Step 3: Formula: vf = vi + g t = 0 + 10 x 5 = 50 m/s. Final answer: height of tower = 125 m; striking velocity = 50 m/s.

Q: 2.10 A cricket ball is hit so that it travels straight up in the air. An observer notes that it took 3 seconds to reach the highest point. What was the initial velocity of the ball? If the ball was hit 1 m above the ground, how high did it rise from the ground?

Given: time to highest point t = 3 s; at the highest point vf = 0; g = 10 m/s^2 (acting downward, taken as -10 m/s^2 for upward motion). Step 1: Formula: vf = vi - g t. Step 2: Substitute: 0 = vi - 10 x 3, so vi = 30 m/s. Step 3: Formula: 2 g h = vf^2 - vi^2 with signs for upward motion: -2 x 10 x h = 0 - (30)^2, so h = 900 / 20 = 45 m. Step 4: The ball was hit 1 m above the ground, so total height from the ground = 45 + 1 = 46 m. Final answer: initial velocity = 30 m/s; maximum height from the ground = 46 m.

mcqs.q: With the scale 1 cm = 100 m/s, a velocity of 400 m/s making an angle of 60 degrees with the x-axis is represented by a line of length:
options: 4 cm, drawn at 60 degrees above the x-axis with an arrowhead
mcqs.why: Given: magnitude 400 m/s, scale 1 cm = 100 m/s. Length = 400 / 100 = 4 cm. Draw a 4 cm line at 60 degrees above the x-axis with an arrowhead. (For the 50 N force at 120 degrees with scale 1 cm = 10 N: length = 50 / 10 = 5 cm, drawn at 120 degrees from the x-axis.) Result: 4 cm line at 60 degrees.

mcqs.q: A car moves with an average speed of 72 km/h. The time it takes to cover a distance of 360 km is:
mcqs.why: Given: average speed v = 72 km/h, distance S = 360 km. Formula: t = S / v. Substitution: t = 360 km / 72 km/h = 5 h. Result: 5 hours.

mcqs.q: A truck starts from rest and reaches a velocity of 90 km/h in 50 s. Its average acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Given: vi = 0, vf = 90 km/h, t = 50 s. Convert: vf = 90 x 1000 / 3600 = 25 m/s. Formula: a = (vf - vi) / t. Substitution: a = (25 - 0) / 50 = 0.5. Result: average acceleration = 0.5 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A car moving at 5 m/s accelerates at 1.5 m/s^2. Its velocity after 5 s is:
mcqs.why: Given: vi = 5 m/s, a = 1.5 m/s^2, t = 5 s. Formula (first equation of motion): vf = vi + a t. Substitution: vf = 5 + 1.5 x 5 = 5 + 7.5 = 12.5. Result: velocity after 5 s = 12.5 m/s.

mcqs.q: A motorcycle initially travelling at 18 km/h accelerates at a constant rate of 2 m/s^2. The distance it goes in 10 s is:
mcqs.why: Given: vi = 18 km/h, a = 2 m/s^2, t = 10 s. Convert: vi = 18 x 1000 / 3600 = 5 m/s. Formula (second equation of motion): S = vi t + (1/2) a t^2. Substitution: S = 5 x 10 + (1/2) x 2 x (10)^2 = 50 + 100 = 150. Result: distance covered = 150 m.

mcqs.q: A wagon moving at 54 km/h is braked and covers 25 m before stopping. Its acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Given: vi = 54 km/h, vf = 0, S = 25 m. Convert: vi = 54 x 1000 / 3600 = 15 m/s. Formula (third equation of motion): 2 a S = vf^2 - vi^2. Substitution: 2 x a x 25 = 0 - (15)^2 = -225, so a = -225 / 50 = -4.5. Result: acceleration = -4.5 m/s^2; the negative sign shows retardation of 4.5 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. The time it takes to reach the ground is:
mcqs.why: Given: h = 45 m, vi = 0, g = 10 m/s^2. Formula: h = vi t + (1/2) g t^2. Substitution: 45 = 0 + (1/2) x 10 x t^2 = 5 t^2, so t^2 = 9 and t = 3 s. Result: time = 3 s (and vf = vi + g t = 0 + 10 x 3 = 30 m/s on hitting the ground).

mcqs.q: A car travels 10 km at an average velocity of 20 m/s, then travels 0.8 km in the same direction at an average velocity of 4 m/s. Its average velocity for the total journey is:
mcqs.why: Given: S1 = 10 km = 10000 m at v1 = 20 m/s; S2 = 0.8 km = 800 m at v2 = 4 m/s, same direction. Times: t1 = 10000 / 20 = 500 s; t2 = 800 / 4 = 200 s. Total displacement = 10800 m; total time = 700 s. Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 10800 / 700 = 15.4 m/s. Result: 15.4 m/s.

mcqs.q: A ball dropped from the top of a tower reaches the ground in 5 s. The height of the tower is:
mcqs.why: Given: t = 5 s, vi = 0, g = 10 m/s^2. Formula: h = vi t + (1/2) g t^2. Substitution: h = 0 + (1/2) x 10 x (5)^2 = 5 x 25 = 125 m. Result: height of tower = 125 m (and striking velocity vf = vi + g t = 0 + 10 x 5 = 50 m/s).

mcqs.q: A cricket ball hit straight up takes 3 s to reach the highest point. Its initial velocity was:
mcqs.why: Given: time to highest point t = 3 s, at the highest point vf = 0, g = 10 m/s^2 taken as -10 m/s^2 for upward motion. Formula: vf = vi - g t. Substitution: 0 = vi - 10 x 3, so vi = 30 m/s. Result: initial velocity = 30 m/s (maximum height above the hit point h = (30)^2 / (2 x 10) = 45 m, i.e. 45 + 1 = 46 m from the ground).

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: When we kick a stone, we get hurt. This is due to:

(a) inertia (b) velocity (c) momentum (d) reaction
Correct answer: reaction The stone exerts an equal and opposite reaction force on the foot.

Q: An object will continue its motion with constant acceleration until:

(a) the resultant force on it begins to decrease. (b) the resultant force on it is zero. (c) the resultant force on it begins to increase. (d) the resultant force is at right angle to its tangential velocity.
Correct answer: the resultant force on it is zero.

Q: Which of the following is a non-contact force?

(a) Friction (b) Air resistance (c) Electrostatic force (d) Tension in the string
Correct answer: Electrostatic force

Q: A ball with initial momentum p hits a solid wall and bounces back with the same velocity. Its momentum p' after collision will be:

(a) p' = p (b) p' = -p (c) p' = 2p (d) p' = -2p
Correct answer: p' = -p The velocity reverses direction while its magnitude stays the same, so the momentum reverses sign.

Q: A particle of mass m moving with a velocity v collides with another particle of the same mass at rest. The velocity of the first particle after collision is:

(a) v (b) -v (c) 0 (d) -1/2
Correct answer: 0 In an elastic head-on collision between equal masses the velocities are exchanged: the moving particle stops and the particle at rest moves off with velocity v.

Q: Conservation of linear momentum is equivalent to:

(a) Newton's first law of motion (b) Newton's second law of motion (c) Newton's third law of motion (d) None of these
Correct answer: Newton's third law of motion During a collision the bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other for the same time, so their impulses and momentum changes are equal and opposite and cancel out.

Q: An object with a mass of 5 kg moves at constant velocity of 10 m s^-1. A constant force then acts for 5 seconds on the object and gives it a velocity of 2 m s^-1 in the opposite direction. The force acting on the object is:

(a) 5 N (b) -10 N (c) -12 N (d) -15 N
Correct answer: -12 N Using F = m(v - u) / t = 5 x (-2 - 10) / 5 = -12 N, the negative sign showing the force acts opposite to the original motion.

Q: A large force acts on an object for a very short interval of time. In this case, it is easy to determine:

(a) magnitude of force (b) time interval (c) product of force and time (d) none of these
Correct answer: product of force and time Impulse is the product of force and time, and it is equal to the total change in momentum of the body.

Q: A lubricant is usually introduced between two surfaces to decrease friction. The lubricant:

(a) decreases temperature (b) acts as ball bearings (c) prevents direct contact of the surfaces (d) provides rolling friction
Correct answer: prevents direct contact of the surfaces

Q: Note: Why does the first particle stop?

In an elastic head-on collision between equal masses the velocities are exchanged: the moving particle stops and the particle at rest moves off with velocity v. That is why the first particle's velocity after the collision is zero.

mcqs.q: When we kick a stone, we get hurt. This is due to:
mcqs.why: By Newton's third law, the stone exerts an equal and opposite reaction force on the foot, and that reaction is what hurts when we kick it.

mcqs.q: An object will continue its motion with constant acceleration until:
options: the resultant force on it begins to decrease.
the resultant force on it is zero.
the resultant force on it begins to increase.
the resultant force is at right angle to its tangential velocity.
mcqs.why: Acceleration is produced by the resultant force through F = ma. When the resultant force on the object becomes zero, there is no net force left to sustain the acceleration.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-contact force?
mcqs.why: Electrostatic force acts between charged bodies without physical contact, whereas friction, air resistance and tension in a string are contact forces that act only when bodies touch.

mcqs.q: A ball with initial momentum p hits a solid wall and bounces back with the same velocity. Its momentum p' after collision will be:
mcqs.why: The ball bounces back with the same speed, so its velocity reverses direction. Since momentum p = mv reverses sign with the velocity, the momentum after collision is p' = -p.

mcqs.q: A particle of mass m moving with a velocity v collides with another particle of the same mass at rest. The velocity of the first particle after collision is:
mcqs.why: In an elastic head-on collision between equal masses the velocities are exchanged: the moving particle stops and the particle at rest moves off with velocity v, so the first particle's velocity is 0.

mcqs.q: Conservation of linear momentum is equivalent to:
mcqs.why: Conservation of linear momentum follows from Newton's third law: during a collision the bodies exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so their momentum changes cancel and total momentum stays constant.

mcqs.q: An object with a mass of 5 kg moves at constant velocity of 10 m s^-1. A constant force then acts for 5 seconds on the object and gives it a velocity of 2 m s^-1 in the opposite direction. The force acting on the object is:
mcqs.why: Force equals rate of change of momentum: F = m(v - u) / t = 5 x (-2 - 10) / 5 = 5 x (-12) / 5 = -12 N, the negative sign showing the force acts opposite to the original velocity.

mcqs.q: A large force acts on an object for a very short interval of time. In this case, it is easy to determine:
mcqs.why: A large force acting for a very short time produces an impulse, which is the product of force and time (F x delta t) and equals the total change in momentum, so that product is what can be determined.

mcqs.q: A lubricant is usually introduced between two surfaces to decrease friction. The lubricant:
options: prevents direct contact of the surfaces
mcqs.why: A lubricant forms a layer between the two surfaces and prevents their direct contact, so the surfaces do not rub directly against each other and friction decreases.

mcqs.q: What is the impulse of a force?
options: The product of the force and the time for which it acts
The product of mass and acceleration
The product of mass and velocity
The force divided by the mass
mcqs.why: The chapter defines impulse as the product of the force and the time for which it acts, impulse = F x delta t, equal to the total change in momentum, with unit newton second (N s).

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3.1 What kind of changes in motion may be produced by a force?

A force can start a body moving, stop it, speed it up or slow it down (change the magnitude of its velocity), change the direction of its motion, and change its shape or size. In short, a force produces acceleration or deformation in the body on which it acts.

Q: 3.2 Give 5 examples of contact forces.

Friction (when a book is pushed on a table), the push or pull of our muscles (lifting a bag), tension in a string or rope, the normal reaction of a surface (a book resting on a table), and air or water resistance on a moving body. Any five such forces that act only when the bodies touch are contact forces.

Q: 3.3 An object moves with constant velocity in free space. How long will the object continue to move with this velocity?

Forever, in principle. In free space there is no friction or other net external force, so by Newton's first law the object keeps its state of uniform motion with the same velocity indefinitely, until some external force acts on it.

Q: 3.4 Define impulse of force.

The impulse of a force is the product of the force and the time for which it acts: impulse = F x delta t. It is equal to the total change in momentum of the body, m x delta v, and its unit is the newton second (N s).

Q: 3.5 Why has not Newton's first law been proved on the Earth?

Newton's first law describes a body moving forever without any force acting on it. On Earth such a situation cannot be produced: friction and air resistance act on every moving body and cannot be completely removed, so a body always slows down and stops. The law is therefore verified indirectly, not proved by a direct experiment on Earth.

Q: 3.6 When sitting in a car which suddenly accelerates from rest, you are pushed back into the seat, why?

Because of inertia. Your body is at rest with the car; when the car suddenly accelerates forward, the lower part of your body moves with the seat, but the upper part tends to remain at rest (inertia of rest), so you appear to be pushed back into the seat.

Q: 3.7 The force expressed in Newton's second law is a net force. Why is it so?

Several forces may act on a body at the same time (push, weight, friction, reaction). The acceleration produced depends not on any single force but on their vector sum, so the F in F = ma is the net (resultant) force. Only the net force changes the momentum of the body.

Q: 3.8 How can you show that rolling friction is lesser than the sliding friction?

Drag a heavy box across the floor: it is hard to move. Now place round poles or rollers under the same box (or lift it onto a wheeled trolley): it moves with a much smaller push. The load is the same, only sliding is replaced by rolling, which shows that rolling friction is much less than sliding friction.

Q: 3.9 Define terminal velocity of an object.

When an object falls through air, air resistance increases with its speed. The constant maximum velocity reached when the upward air resistance becomes equal to the downward weight of the object, so that the net force and acceleration become zero, is called its terminal velocity. The object then falls safely at this constant velocity.

Q: 3.10 An astronaut walking in space wants to return to his spaceship by firing a hand rocket. In what direction does he fire the rocket?

In the direction away from the spaceship. The rocket's gases are fired away from the ship, and by Newton's third law (conservation of momentum) the reaction pushes the astronaut in the opposite direction, back towards the spaceship.

mcqs.q: What does a force produce in the body on which it acts?
options: Only a change in its mass
mcqs.why: A force can start or stop a body, speed it up or slow it down, change the direction of its motion, and change its shape or size; in short, it produces acceleration or deformation.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is given in the chapter as a contact force?
mcqs.why: Contact forces act only when bodies touch. The chapter lists friction, the push or pull of muscles, tension in a string or rope, the normal reaction of a surface, and air or water resistance as contact forces.

mcqs.q: An object moves with constant velocity in free space, where no net external force acts. How long will it continue with this velocity?
options: Until friction in space stops it
Forever, until some external force acts on it
mcqs.why: In free space there is no friction or other net external force, so by Newton's first law the object keeps its state of uniform motion with the same velocity indefinitely, until an external force acts.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of impulse?
mcqs.why: Impulse = F x delta t and equals the total change in momentum, m x delta v. The chapter states its unit is the newton second (N s).

mcqs.q: Why has Newton's first law not been proved by a direct experiment on Earth?
options: Because bodies have no inertia on Earth
Because friction and air resistance act on every moving body and cannot be completely removed
Because gravity does not act on Earth
Because velocity cannot be measured on Earth
mcqs.why: On Earth friction and air resistance act on every moving body and cannot be completely removed, so a body always slows down and stops; the first law is therefore verified indirectly, not proved directly.

mcqs.q: When a car suddenly accelerates from rest, a passenger is pushed back into the seat because of:
mcqs.why: The lower part of the body moves with the seat, but the upper part tends to remain at rest due to inertia of rest, so the passenger appears to be pushed back into the seat.

mcqs.q: In Newton's second law, F = ma, the force F is:
options: Only the weight of the body
mcqs.why: Several forces may act on a body at the same time, and the acceleration depends on their vector sum, so F in F = ma is the net (resultant) force; only the net force changes the momentum of the body.

mcqs.q: Compared with sliding friction, rolling friction is:
mcqs.why: A heavy box dragged across the floor is hard to move, but on round poles, rollers or a wheeled trolley it moves with a much smaller push for the same load, showing rolling friction is much less than sliding friction.

mcqs.q: An object falling through air reaches terminal velocity when:
options: Air resistance becomes equal to its weight, so net force and acceleration become zero
mcqs.why: Air resistance increases with speed until the upward air resistance equals the downward weight; the net force and acceleration then become zero and the object falls at this constant maximum velocity.

mcqs.q: An astronaut in space wants to return to his spaceship by firing a hand rocket. In which direction should he fire it?
options: In the direction of his motion away from the ship's gases
mcqs.why: The rocket's gases are fired away from the ship, and by Newton's third law (conservation of momentum) the reaction pushes the astronaut in the opposite direction, back towards the spaceship.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3.1 Two ice skaters weighing 60 kg and 80 kg push off against each other on a frictionless ice track. The 60 kg skater gains a velocity of 4 m s^-1. Considering all the relevant calculations involved, explain how Newton's third law applies to this situation.

Step 1: When the skaters push, each exerts a force on the other; by Newton's third law the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, acting on two different bodies. Step 2: Total momentum before the push is zero (both at rest), and no external force acts (frictionless ice), so total momentum stays zero: 60 x 4 + 80 x v = 0. Step 3: 240 + 80 v = 0, so v = -3 m/s. The 80 kg skater moves at 3 m/s in the opposite direction to the 60 kg skater. The heavier skater gets the smaller speed, exactly as the third law with conservation of momentum requires.

Q: 3.2 Inflatable airbags are installed in the vehicles as safety equipment. In terms of momentum, what is the advantage of airbags over seatbelts?

Stopping a passenger means changing his momentum to zero. Force = change of momentum / time. A seatbelt alone stops the body in a very short time, so the force is large. An airbag inflates and yields as the body sinks into it, stretching the stopping time; the same change of momentum is then produced by a much smaller, safer force, spread over the chest and face instead of cutting in like a belt.

Q: 3.3 A horse refuses to pull a cart. The horse argues, "according to Newton's third law, whatever force I exert on the cart, the cart will exert an equal and opposite force on me. Since the net force will be zero, therefore, I have no chance of accelerating (pulling) the cart." What is wrong with this reasoning?

The error is that action and reaction act on two different bodies, so they never cancel each other on one body. The force on the cart acts on the cart, and the reaction acts on the horse. The cart accelerates if the pull on it exceeds friction on it; the horse accelerates because it pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes it forwards. Whether the system moves depends on these external forces (especially friction with the ground), not on the internal action-reaction pair cancelling.

Q: 3.4 When a cricket ball hits high, a fielder tries to catch it. While holding the ball he/she draws hands backward. Why?

To catch the ball its momentum must be reduced to zero. Impulse = change of momentum = force x time. By drawing the hands backward, the fielder increases the time over which the ball stops, so the force on the hands is much smaller and the catch does not hurt or drop.

Q: 3.5 When someone jumps from a small boat onto the river bank, why does the jumper often fall into the water? Explain.

As the jumper pushes off, he exerts a backward force on the boat; by Newton's third law the boat is pushed away from the bank into the river (conservation of momentum). The gap between boat and bank widens while he is in the air, so he may land short of the bank and fall into the water.

Q: 3.6 Imagine that if friction vanishes suddenly from everything, then what could be the scenario of daily life activities?

Daily life would become almost impossible. We could not walk or run, because our feet would slip without grip; vehicles could neither start, turn nor stop, and brakes and tyres would be useless. Nails, screws, knots and belts would not hold, we could not grip a pen or a glass, and anything once moving would keep sliding until it hit something. Friction, though it wastes some energy, is essential for controlled motion.

mcqs.q: Two skaters of 60 kg and 80 kg push off each other on frictionless ice. The 60 kg skater gains 4 m/s. What is the velocity of the 80 kg skater?
mcqs.why: Total momentum before the push is zero and no external force acts, so it stays zero: 60 x 4 + 80 x v = 0, giving 240 + 80v = 0 and v = -3 m/s; the negative sign means 3 m/s in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: When the two skaters push each other, the forces they exert on each other are:
options: Equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and acting on two different bodies
Equal and acting on the same body, so they cancel
Unequal, the heavier skater exerting the larger force
Exerted by only one skater on the other
mcqs.why: By Newton's third law, when the skaters push, each exerts a force on the other; the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and they act on two different bodies.

mcqs.q: In terms of momentum, the advantage of an airbag over a seatbelt alone is that the airbag:
options: Increases the change of momentum of the passenger
Stretches the stopping time, so the same change of momentum is produced by a much smaller force
Stops the body in a shorter time
