Increases the force on the chest and face
mcqs.why: Force = change of momentum / time. An airbag inflates and yields as the body sinks into it, stretching the stopping time, so the same change of momentum is produced by a much smaller, safer force spread over the chest and face.

mcqs.q: A horse argues that action and reaction cancel, so it can never pull a cart. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Action and reaction act on two different bodies, so they never cancel each other on one body
Newton's third law does not apply to horses
Friction never acts on a cart
The cart exerts no force on the horse
mcqs.why: The force on the cart acts on the cart and the reaction acts on the horse, so they do not cancel on one body. The cart accelerates if the pull on it exceeds friction on it, and the system moves according to the external forces.

mcqs.q: How does the horse itself accelerate when pulling a cart?
options: The cart pulls it forward with a larger force
Action cancels reaction on the horse
It pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes it forwards
Friction on the cart pushes the horse
mcqs.why: The horse pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes it forwards. Whether the system moves depends on these external forces, especially friction with the ground, not on the internal action-reaction pair cancelling.

mcqs.q: A fielder draws his hands backward while catching a fast cricket ball in order to:
options: Increase the stopping force on his hands
Decrease the time in which the ball stops
Increase the time in which the ball stops, so the force on his hands is smaller
Increase the momentum of the ball
mcqs.why: Impulse = change of momentum = force x time. By drawing the hands backward the fielder increases the time over which the ball stops, so the force on the hands is much smaller and the catch does not hurt or drop.

mcqs.q: When a person jumps from a small boat towards the river bank, why does he often fall into the water?
options: He pushes the boat away from the bank, so the gap between boat and bank widens while he is in the air
The water pulls him down before he jumps
The boat moves towards the bank under him
mcqs.why: As the jumper pushes off, he exerts a backward force on the boat; by Newton's third law the boat is pushed away from the bank into the river, the gap widens while he is in the air, and he may land short of the bank.

mcqs.q: If friction suddenly vanished from everything, walking and running would become:
options: Almost impossible, because our feet would slip without grip
mcqs.why: Without friction our feet would slip without grip; vehicles could neither start, turn nor stop, nails, screws, knots and belts would not hold, and we could not grip a pen or a glass, so daily life would become almost impossible.

mcqs.q: If friction suddenly vanished, brakes and tyres of vehicles would be:
options: Useless, because vehicles could neither start, turn nor stop
mcqs.why: Vehicles move, turn and stop because of friction: the driving wheels push the road backward and road friction pushes the vehicle forward. Without friction the wheels would simply spin and brakes and tyres would be useless.

mcqs.q: To reduce the force needed for a given change of momentum, as in airbags and a fielder's catch, one should:
options: Decrease the time of the change
Increase the time of the change
mcqs.why: Since force = change of momentum / time, increasing the time over which the momentum changes produces the same change with a much smaller force; this is the principle behind both airbags and drawing the hands backward in a catch.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3.1 Explain the concept of force by practical examples.

A force is a push or a pull that starts, stops or changes the motion of a body, or changes its shape. Examples: pushing a trolley starts it moving; catching a ball stops it; pressing the accelerator speeds a car up; the pull of a magnet moves a nail without touching it; squeezing a sponge changes its shape. In every case some agent exerts the push or pull, and the effect is a change in the state of motion or shape of the body.

Q: 3.2 Describe Newton's laws of motion.

First law: a body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. This defines inertia. Second law: when a net force acts on a body, it produces an acceleration in the direction of the force, directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass: F = ma. Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; action and reaction act on two different bodies.

Q: 3.3 Define momentum and express Newton's 2nd law of motion in terms of change in momentum.

Momentum is the product of the mass of a body and its velocity: p = m v. It is a vector quantity with unit kg m/s. Newton's second law in momentum form: the net force acting on a body is equal to the rate of change of its momentum, F = (mv - mu) / t = change in momentum / time taken. This form is the original statement of the law and also covers bodies whose mass changes.

Q: 3.4 State and explain the principle of conservation of momentum.

Principle: if no external force acts on an isolated system, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant; the final total momentum is equal to the initial total momentum. Explanation: during a collision the bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other for the same time (third law), so their impulses and momentum changes are equal and opposite and cancel out. Example: a gun recoils so that the forward momentum of the bullet equals the backward momentum of the gun; the total stays zero, as before firing.

Q: 3.5 Describe the motion of a block on a table taking into account the friction between the two surfaces. What is the static friction and kinetic friction?

Push a block gently on a table: at first it does not move, because static friction between the surfaces balances the push. Static friction is the resisting force between two surfaces before motion starts; its maximum value is called limiting friction. Push harder and the block starts sliding; friction still opposes the motion but is now slightly smaller: this is kinetic friction, the friction during motion. If the push is withdrawn the block slows down and stops because kinetic friction keeps acting against its motion. Static friction is generally greater than kinetic friction, which is why starting motion is harder than keeping it going.

Q: 3.6 Explain the effect of friction on the motion of vehicles in context of tyre surface and braking force.

A vehicle moves because of friction: the driving wheels push the road backward and the road's friction pushes the vehicle forward; without friction the wheels would simply spin. Tyre treads increase grip (friction) with the road, especially on wet roads where they also channel water away. When brakes are applied, friction between brake parts stops the wheels, and friction between tyres and road (the braking force) slows the vehicle; worn tyres or a slippery road reduce this friction, lengthen the stopping distance and can cause skidding.

mcqs.q: Squeezing a sponge with the hand is an example of a force that:
options: Changes the shape of a body
Changes only the colour of a body
Creates new mass in a body
Removes the inertia of a body
mcqs.why: A force is a push or a pull that starts, stops or changes the motion of a body, or changes its shape; squeezing a sponge changes its shape, just as pushing a trolley starts it moving and catching a ball stops it.

mcqs.q: According to Newton's first law, a body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless it is acted upon by:
mcqs.why: The first law states that a body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force; this property of a body is its inertia.

mcqs.q: Newton's second law of motion is expressed by the equation:
mcqs.why: The second law states that a net force produces an acceleration in the direction of the force, directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass, which is expressed as F = ma.

mcqs.q: According to Newton's third law, action and reaction act on:
options: The same body, so they cancel
Bodies moving in the same direction
mcqs.why: The third law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, and action and reaction act on two different bodies, so they do not cancel each other on one body.

mcqs.q: The momentum of a body is defined as:
options: Mass multiplied by velocity, p = mv
mcqs.why: Momentum is the product of the mass of a body and its velocity, p = mv. It is a vector quantity with unit kg m/s.

mcqs.q: Newton's second law in momentum form states that the net force on a body is equal to:
options: The rate of change of its momentum
The rate of change of its mass
mcqs.why: In momentum form, F = (mv - mu) / t = change in momentum / time taken, so the net force equals the rate of change of momentum; this form also covers bodies whose mass changes.

mcqs.q: The total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant when:
options: A strong external force acts on it
No external force acts on the system
The mass of the system changes rapidly
All bodies in it stick together
mcqs.why: The principle of conservation of momentum states that if no external force acts on an isolated system, the total linear momentum remains constant; the final total momentum equals the initial total momentum.

mcqs.q: When a gun is fired, it recoils so that:
options: The gun moves forward with the bullet
The total momentum becomes twice the bullet's momentum
The forward momentum of the bullet equals the backward momentum of the gun, and the total stays zero as before firing
mcqs.why: Before firing the total momentum is zero. The gun recoils so that the forward momentum of the bullet equals the backward momentum of the gun, and the total momentum stays zero, exactly as the conservation principle requires.

mcqs.q: For a block pushed gently on a table, static friction compared with kinetic friction is generally:
mcqs.why: Static friction acts before motion starts and its maximum value is limiting friction; once the block slides, kinetic friction is slightly smaller. Static friction is generally greater than kinetic friction, which is why starting motion is harder than keeping it going.

mcqs.q: A vehicle moves forward on a road because:
options: The driving wheels push the road backward and the road's friction pushes the vehicle forward
Friction pushes the driving wheels backward only
Tyre treads remove all friction with the road
The brakes push the vehicle forward
mcqs.why: The driving wheels push the road backward and the road's friction pushes the vehicle forward; without friction the wheels would simply spin. Tyre treads increase grip with the road, especially on wet roads.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3.1 A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find: (a) the acceleration produced in the block. (b) the velocity of block after 5 seconds.

Given: mass m = 10 kg; force F = 5 N; time t = 5 s; initial velocity vi = 0. Step 1: Formula: F = m a, so a = F / m. Step 2: a = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2. Step 3: Formula: vf = vi + a t = 0 + 0.5 x 5 = 2.5 m/s. Final answer: (a) acceleration = 0.5 m/s^2 (b) velocity after 5 s = 2.5 m/s.

Q: 3.2 The mass of a person is 80 kg. What will be his weight on the Earth? What will be his weight on the Moon? The value of acceleration due to gravity of Moon is 1.6 m s^-2.

Given: mass m = 80 kg; g on Earth = 10 m/s^2; g on Moon = 1.6 m/s^2. Step 1: Formula: weight W = m g. Step 2: On Earth: W = 80 x 10 = 800 N. Step 3: On the Moon: W = 80 x 1.6 = 128 N. Final answer: weight on Earth = 800 N; weight on the Moon = 128 N. (The mass stays 80 kg at both places.)

Q: 3.3 What force is required to increase the velocity of 800 kg car from 10 m s^-1 to 30 m s^-1 in 10 seconds?

Given: mass m = 800 kg; initial velocity vi = 10 m/s; final velocity vf = 30 m/s; time t = 10 s. Step 1: Change of velocity = 30 - 10 = 20 m/s. Step 2: Formula: F = m (vf - vi) / t. Step 3: F = 800 x 20 / 10 = 1600 N. Final answer: force required = 1600 N.

Q: 3.4 A 5 g bullet is fired by a gun. The bullet moves with a velocity of 300 m s^-1. If the mass of the gun is 10 kg, find the recoil speed of the gun.

Given: bullet mass m1 = 5 g = 0.005 kg; bullet velocity v1 = 300 m/s; gun mass m2 = 10 kg. Step 1: Total momentum before firing is zero, and it stays zero (conservation of momentum): m1 v1 + m2 v2 = 0. Step 2: 0.005 x 300 + 10 x v2 = 0, so 1.5 + 10 v2 = 0. Step 3: v2 = -1.5 / 10 = -0.15 m/s. Final answer: recoil speed of the gun = 0.15 m/s; the negative sign shows it moves opposite to the bullet.

Q: 3.5 An astronaut weighs 70 kg. He throws a wrench of mass 300 g at a speed of 3.5 m s^-1. Determine: (a) the speed of astronaut as he recoils away from the wrench. (b) the distance covered by the astronaut in 30 minutes.

Given: astronaut mass M = 70 kg; wrench mass m = 300 g = 0.3 kg; wrench speed v = 3.5 m/s; time = 30 min = 1800 s. Step 1: Conservation of momentum: M V + m v = 0, so 70 V + 0.3 x 3.5 = 0. Step 2: V = -1.05 / 70 = -0.015 = -1.5 x 10^-2 m/s. Step 3: Distance = speed x time = 0.015 x 1800 = 27 m. Final answer: (a) recoil speed = 1.5 x 10^-2 m/s away from the wrench (b) distance in 30 minutes = 27 m.

Q: 3.6 A 6.5 x 10^3 kg bogie of a goods train is moving with a velocity of 0.8 m s^-1. Another bogie of mass 9.2 x 10^3 kg coming from behind with a velocity of 1.2 m s^-1 collides with the first one and couples to it. Find the common velocity of the two bogies after they become coupled.

Given: m1 = 6.5 x 10^3 kg, v1 = 0.8 m/s; m2 = 9.2 x 10^3 kg, v2 = 1.2 m/s; after coupling both move with common velocity V. Step 1: Formula (conservation of momentum): m1 v1 + m2 v2 = (m1 + m2) V. Step 2: Substitute: 6500 x 0.8 + 9200 x 1.2 = 5200 + 11040 = 16240. Step 3: Total mass = 6500 + 9200 = 15700 kg. Step 4: V = 16240 / 15700 = 1.03 m/s. Final answer: common velocity = 1.03 m/s.

Q: 3.7 A cyclist weighing 55 kg rides a bicycle of mass 5 kg. He starts from rest and applies a force of 90 N for 8 seconds. Then he continues at a constant speed for another 8 seconds. Calculate the total distance travelled by the cyclist.

Given: total mass m = 55 + 5 = 60 kg; force F = 90 N; first time t1 = 8 s; second time t2 = 8 s; starts from rest. Step 1: Acceleration a = F / m = 90 / 60 = 1.5 m/s^2. Step 2: Speed reached: vf = 0 + 1.5 x 8 = 12 m/s. Step 3: Distance in first part: S1 = (1/2) a t1^2 = 0.5 x 1.5 x 64 = 48 m. Step 4: Distance in second part at constant speed: S2 = 12 x 8 = 96 m. Step 5: Total distance = 48 + 96 = 144 m. Final answer: 144 m.

Q: 3.8 A ball of mass 0.4 kg is dropped on the floor from a height of 1.8 m. The ball rebounds straight upward to a height of 0.8 m. What is the magnitude and direction of the impulse applied to the ball by the floor?

Given: mass m = 0.4 kg; drop height 1.8 m; rebound height 0.8 m; g = 10 m/s^2; take upward as positive. Step 1: Speed on reaching the floor: v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 1.8) = sqrt(36) = 6 m/s, so initial velocity = -6 m/s. Step 2: Speed of leaving the floor: v = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.8) = sqrt(16) = 4 m/s, so final velocity = +4 m/s. Step 3: Impulse = change of momentum = m (vf - vi) = 0.4 x (4 - (-6)) = 0.4 x 10 = 4 N s. Final answer: impulse = 4 N s, directed upward.

Q: 3.9 Two balls of masses 0.2 kg and 0.4 kg are moving towards each other with velocities 20 m s^-1 and 5 m s^-1 respectively. After collision, the velocity of 0.2 kg ball becomes 6 m s^-1. What will be the velocity of 0.4 kg ball?

Given: m1 = 0.2 kg moving at 20 m/s; m2 = 0.4 kg moving towards it at 5 m/s; after collision the 0.2 kg ball moves at 6 m/s. Take the direction of the 0.2 kg ball as positive, so the 0.4 kg ball's initial velocity is -5 m/s. Step 1: Total momentum before = 0.2 x 20 + 0.4 x (-5) = 4 - 2 = 2 kg m/s. Step 2: Conservation of momentum: total after = total before: 0.2 x 6 + 0.4 x v = 2. Step 3: 1.2 + 0.4 v = 2, so 0.4 v = 0.8 and v = 2 m/s. Final answer: the 0.4 kg ball moves at 2 m/s in the direction in which the 0.2 kg ball was originally moving.

mcqs.q: A horizontal force of 5 N acts on a 10 kg block on a smooth surface. The acceleration produced is:
mcqs.why: Given: mass m = 10 kg, force F = 5 N, initial velocity vi = 0, time t = 5 s. Formula: F = ma, so a = F / m. Substitution: a = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2. Result: acceleration = 0.5 m/s^2 (and vf = vi + at = 0 + 0.5 x 5 = 2.5 m/s).

mcqs.q: A person has mass 80 kg. His weight on the Moon, where g = 1.6 m/s^2, is:
mcqs.why: Given: mass m = 80 kg, g on Moon = 1.6 m/s^2, g on Earth = 10 m/s^2. Formula: weight W = mg. Substitution: W = 80 x 1.6 = 128 N. Result: weight on the Moon = 128 N (on Earth W = 80 x 10 = 800 N; the mass stays 80 kg at both places).

mcqs.q: What force is required to increase the velocity of an 800 kg car from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 10 seconds?
mcqs.why: Given: mass m = 800 kg, vi = 10 m/s, vf = 30 m/s, time t = 10 s. Formula: F = m(vf - vi) / t. Substitution: change of velocity = 30 - 10 = 20 m/s, so F = 800 x 20 / 10 = 1600 N. Result: force required = 1600 N.

mcqs.q: A 5 g bullet is fired at 300 m/s from a 10 kg gun. The recoil speed of the gun is:
options: 1.5 m/s, in the direction of the bullet
0.015 m/s, in the direction of the bullet
mcqs.why: Given: bullet mass m1 = 5 g = 0.005 kg, bullet velocity v1 = 300 m/s, gun mass m2 = 10 kg. Formula: conservation of momentum, m1v1 + m2v2 = 0. Substitution: 0.005 x 300 + 10 x v2 = 0, so 1.5 + 10v2 = 0 and v2 = -0.15 m/s. Result: recoil speed = 0.15 m/s, opposite to the bullet.

mcqs.q: A 70 kg astronaut throws a 300 g wrench at 3.5 m/s. His recoil speed is:
options: 1.5 x 10^-2 m/s away from the wrench
mcqs.why: Given: astronaut mass M = 70 kg, wrench mass m = 300 g = 0.3 kg, wrench speed v = 3.5 m/s. Formula: conservation of momentum, MV + mv = 0. Substitution: 70V + 0.3 x 3.5 = 0, so V = -1.05 / 70 = -0.015 m/s. Result: recoil speed = 1.5 x 10^-2 m/s away from the wrench.

mcqs.q: The astronaut in the previous situation recoils at 0.015 m/s. The distance he covers in 30 minutes is:
mcqs.why: Given: recoil speed = 0.015 m/s, time = 30 min = 1800 s. Formula: distance = speed x time. Substitution: distance = 0.015 x 1800 = 27. Result: distance covered in 30 minutes = 27 m.

mcqs.q: A 6.5 x 10^3 kg bogie moving at 0.8 m/s is coupled to a 9.2 x 10^3 kg bogie moving at 1.2 m/s in the same direction. Their common velocity after coupling is:
mcqs.why: Given: m1 = 6.5 x 10^3 kg, v1 = 0.8 m/s; m2 = 9.2 x 10^3 kg, v2 = 1.2 m/s. Formula: conservation of momentum, m1v1 + m2v2 = (m1 + m2)V. Substitution: 6500 x 0.8 + 9200 x 1.2 = 5200 + 11040 = 16240, total mass = 15700 kg, so V = 16240 / 15700 = 1.03 m/s. Result: common velocity = 1.03 m/s.

mcqs.q: A 55 kg cyclist on a 5 kg bicycle starts from rest, applies 90 N for 8 s, then continues at constant speed for another 8 s. The total distance travelled is:
mcqs.why: Given: total mass m = 55 + 5 = 60 kg, force F = 90 N, t1 = 8 s, t2 = 8 s, starts from rest. Formula: a = F / m = 90 / 60 = 1.5 m/s^2. Substitution: speed reached vf = 0 + 1.5 x 8 = 12 m/s; S1 = (1/2)at1^2 = 0.5 x 1.5 x 64 = 48 m; S2 = 12 x 8 = 96 m. Result: total distance = 48 + 96 = 144 m.

mcqs.q: A 0.4 kg ball dropped from 1.8 m rebounds to 0.8 m (g = 10 m/s^2). The impulse applied to the ball by the floor is:
mcqs.why: Given: mass m = 0.4 kg, drop height 1.8 m, rebound height 0.8 m, g = 10 m/s^2, upward positive. Formula: speed from v = sqrt(2gh); impulse = m(vf - vi). Substitution: reaching speed = sqrt(2 x 10 x 1.8) = sqrt(36) = 6 m/s, so vi = -6 m/s; leaving speed = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.8) = sqrt(16) = 4 m/s, so vf = +4 m/s; impulse = 0.4 x (4 - (-6)) = 0.4 x 10 = 4 N s. Result: impulse = 4 N s, directed upward.

mcqs.q: A 0.2 kg ball moving at 20 m/s collides with a 0.4 kg ball moving towards it at 5 m/s. After collision the 0.2 kg ball moves at 6 m/s. The velocity of the 0.4 kg ball after collision is:
options: -2 m/s, opposite to the 0.2 kg ball's original direction
2 m/s in the direction in which the 0.2 kg ball was originally moving
20 m/s in the direction of the 0.2 kg ball
mcqs.why: Given: m1 = 0.2 kg at 20 m/s, m2 = 0.4 kg moving towards it at 5 m/s (so -5 m/s), after collision the 0.2 kg ball moves at 6 m/s. Formula: conservation of momentum, total momentum before = total after. Substitution: before = 0.2 x 20 + 0.4 x (-5) = 4 - 2 = 2 kg m/s; after: 0.2 x 6 + 0.4v = 2, so 1.2 + 0.4v = 2 and v = 0.8 / 0.4 = 2 m/s. Result: the 0.4 kg ball moves at 2 m/s in the direction in which the 0.2 kg ball was originally moving.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: A particle is simultaneously acted upon by two forces of 4 and 3 newtons. The net force on the particle is:

(a) 1 N (b) between 1 N and 7 N (c) 5 N (d) 7 N
Correct answer: between 1 N and 7 N The net force is largest when the two forces act in the same direction and smallest when they act in opposite directions.

Q: A force F is making an angle of 60 degrees with x-axis. Its y-component is equal to:

(a) F (b) F sin 60 degrees (c) F cos 60 degrees (d) F tan 60 degrees
Correct answer: F sin 60 degrees

Q: Moment of force is called:

(a) moment arm (b) couple (c) couple arm (d) torque
Correct answer: torque

Q: If F1 and F2 are the forces acting on a body and tau is the torque produced in it, the body will be completely in equilibrium, when:

(a) sum F = 0 and sum torque = 0 (b) sum F = 0 and sum torque not zero (c) sum F not zero and sum torque = 0 (d) sum F not zero and sum torque not zero
Correct answer: sum F = 0 and sum torque = 0 Both conditions must hold together for a body to be completely in equilibrium.

Q: A Shopkeeper sells his articles by a balance having unequal arms of the pans. If he puts the weights in the pan having shorter arm, then the customer:

(a) loses (b) gains (c) neither loses nor gains (d) not certain
Correct answer: loses With the weights in the shorter-arm pan, their moment balances a smaller weight of goods in the longer-arm pan, so the customer receives less than the weights indicate.

Q: A man walks on a tight rope. He balances himself by holding a bamboo stick horizontally. It is an application of:

(a) law of conservation of momentum (b) Newton's second law of motion (c) principle of moments (d) Newton's third law of motion
Correct answer: principle of moments The stick helps the walker keep the clockwise and anticlockwise moments balanced about his feet.

Q: In stable equilibrium, the centre of gravity of the body lies:

(a) at the highest position (b) at the lowest position (c) at any position (d) outside the body
Correct answer: at the lowest position In stable equilibrium a slight tilt raises the centre of gravity, so the body returns to its original position.

Q: The centre of mass of a body:

(a) lies always inside the body (b) lies always outside the body (c) lies always on the surface of the body (d) may lie within, outside or on the surface
Correct answer: may lie within, outside or on the surface

Q: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in:

(a) stable equilibrium (b) unstable equilibrium (c) neutral equilibrium (d) dynamic equilibrium
Correct answer: stable equilibrium

Q: Centripetal force is given by:

(a) rF (b) rF cos theta (c) m v^2 / r (d) m v / r^2
Correct answer: m v^2 / r

mcqs.q: A particle is simultaneously acted upon by two forces of 4 and 3 newtons. The net force on the particle is:
mcqs.why: The two forces can add up to at most 4 + 3 = 7 N when they act in the same direction and cancel down to 4 - 3 = 1 N when they act in opposite directions, so the net force must lie between 1 N and 7 N.

mcqs.q: A force F is making an angle of 60 degrees with x-axis. Its y-component is equal to:
mcqs.why: The component of a force F at right angles to the x-axis is the vertical component Fy = F sin theta. With theta = 60 degrees, the y-component is F sin 60 degrees.

mcqs.q: Moment of force is called:
mcqs.why: The moment of a force about an axis, the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from the axis, is called torque: torque = F x d.

mcqs.q: If F1 and F2 are the forces acting on a body and tau is the torque produced in it, the body will be completely in equilibrium, when:
options: sum F = 0 and sum torque not zero
sum F not zero and sum torque = 0
sum F not zero and sum torque not zero
mcqs.why: A body is completely in equilibrium only when both conditions hold together: the vector sum of all forces is zero (sum F = 0) and the vector sum of all torques is zero (sum torque = 0).

mcqs.q: A Shopkeeper sells his articles by a balance having unequal arms of the pans. If he puts the weights in the pan having shorter arm, then the customer:
mcqs.why: Moment is force times arm. The weights sit in the pan with the shorter arm, so their moment balances a smaller weight of goods in the pan with the longer arm; the customer receives less goods than the weights show, so the customer loses.

mcqs.q: A man walks on a tight rope. He balances himself by holding a bamboo stick horizontally. It is an application of:
mcqs.why: By holding the bamboo stick horizontally the walker adjusts and balances the clockwise and anticlockwise moments about his feet, which is exactly the principle of moments used to keep himself in rotational equilibrium.

mcqs.q: In stable equilibrium, the centre of gravity of the body lies:
mcqs.why: In stable equilibrium the centre of gravity lies at the lowest position; a slight tilt raises it, and the body returns to its original position, as with a cone resting on its wide base.

mcqs.q: The centre of mass of a body:
options: lies always on the surface of the body
may lie within, outside or on the surface
mcqs.why: The centre of mass is the point where the whole mass of the body may be supposed to be concentrated. Depending on the shape of the body, this point may lie within the body, outside it, or on its surface.

mcqs.q: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in:
mcqs.why: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in stable equilibrium, because a slight tilt raises its centre of gravity and it returns to its original position.

mcqs.q: Centripetal force is given by:
mcqs.why: Centripetal force is given by Fc = m v^2 / r, where m is the mass, v the speed and r the radius of the circular path; it acts along the radius towards the centre.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4.1 Define like and unlike parallel forces.

Parallel forces whose lines of action are parallel to each other and which act in the same direction are called like parallel forces, e.g. two men pushing a car forwards together. Parallel forces which act in opposite directions are called unlike parallel forces, e.g. two children pulling a rope in opposite directions along parallel lines.

Q: 4.2 What are rectangular components of a vector and their values?

The rectangular components of a vector are its two components at right angles to each other, usually along the x and y axes. For a vector F making an angle theta with the x-axis: horizontal component Fx = F cos theta and vertical component Fy = F sin theta. The vector is the resultant of these two components: F = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).

Q: 4.3 What is the line of action of a force?

The straight line along which a force acts, extended in both directions, is called the line of action of the force. The turning effect of the force about an axis depends on the perpendicular distance of this line from the axis, called the moment arm.

Q: 4.4 Define moment of a force. Prove that torque = rF sin theta, where theta is angle between r and F.

The moment of a force (torque) about an axis is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from the axis: torque = F x d. Proof: let force F act at a point whose position vector from the axis is r, at angle theta between r and F. Only the component of F perpendicular to r, which is F sin theta, turns the body (the component along r, F cos theta, pulls along the line and produces no turning). The perpendicular distance of the line of action from the axis is r sin theta. Hence torque = F x (r sin theta) = r F sin theta, i.e. tau = rF sin theta.

Q: 4.5 With the help of a diagram, show that the resultant force is zero but the resultant torque is not zero.

Apply two equal and opposite parallel forces at two different points of a body, e.g. two 10 N forces, one upward at the left end of a rod and one downward at the right end (a couple). Their resultant force is 10 - 10 = 0, so the body does not translate. But their moments about the centre act in the same rotational sense and add up, giving a non-zero resultant torque that rotates the body. (Draw the rod with the two arrows in the notes.)

Q: 4.6 Identify the state of equilibrium in each case in the figure given below. (a) a cone standing on its base (b) a ball balanced on top of a dome (c) a cylinder lying on its curved side

(a) The cone resting on its wide circular base: stable equilibrium, because a slight tilt raises its centre of gravity and it returns to its original position. (b) The ball resting on top of the dome: unstable equilibrium, because the slightest displacement lowers its centre of gravity and it rolls further away. (c) The cylinder lying on its curved side: neutral equilibrium, because rolling it neither raises nor lowers its centre of gravity and it stays in the new position.

Q: 4.7 Give an example of the body which is moving yet in equilibrium.

A car moving on a straight level road with constant velocity: it is moving, yet the resultant force on it is zero (engine pull balances friction and air resistance), so it is in (dynamic) equilibrium. A ceiling fan rotating at constant speed is another example of rotational equilibrium while moving.

Q: 4.8 Define centre of mass and centre of gravity of a body.

The centre of mass of a body is the point where the whole mass of the body may be supposed to be concentrated. The centre of gravity of a body is the point (inside or outside the body) at which the whole weight of the body acts, i.e. through which the resultant of the gravitational pull on all its particles passes. Near the Earth's surface the two points coincide.

Q: 4.9 What are two basic principles of stability in physics which are applied in designing balancing toys and racing cars?

(1) The centre of gravity should be kept as low as possible. (2) The base of support should be made as wide as possible, so that the vertical line through the centre of gravity stays well inside the base even when tilted. Balancing toys keep a heavy low base, and racing cars are built low and wide, on exactly these two principles.

Q: 4.10 How can you prove that the centripetal force always acts perpendicular to velocity?

Centripetal force keeps changing the direction of velocity while the speed stays constant; if it had any component along the velocity it would change the speed. Its direction is along the radius towards the centre, while the velocity is along the tangent; radius and tangent are at right angles, so the force is always perpendicular to the velocity. This is also why it does no work on the body.

mcqs.q: Parallel forces that act in the same direction, such as two men pushing a car forwards together, are called:
mcqs.why: Parallel forces whose lines of action are parallel to each other and which act in the same direction are called like parallel forces; two men pushing a car forwards together is the chapter's own example.

mcqs.q: For a force F making an angle theta with the x-axis, the horizontal (x) component is:
mcqs.why: The rectangular components of F are Fx = F cos theta along the x-axis and Fy = F sin theta along the y-axis, the two components being at right angles to each other.

mcqs.q: If Fx and Fy are the rectangular components of a force F, the magnitude of F is:
mcqs.why: The vector F is the resultant of its two rectangular components, so by Pythagoras F = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2), with Fx = F cos theta and Fy = F sin theta.

mcqs.q: The line of action of a force is:
options: the perpendicular distance of the force from the axis
the point where the force is applied
the straight line along which the force acts, extended in both directions
the direction in which the body rotates
mcqs.why: The straight line along which a force acts, extended in both directions, is called its line of action; the perpendicular distance of this line from the axis is the moment arm, on which the turning effect depends.

mcqs.q: The torque produced by a force F acting at position r, where theta is the angle between r and F, is:
mcqs.why: Only the component of F perpendicular to r, which is F sin theta, turns the body, and the perpendicular distance of the line of action from the axis is r sin theta, so torque = F x (r sin theta) = rF sin theta.

mcqs.q: In the proof that torque = rF sin theta, the component of the force that produces NO turning effect is:
options: F sin theta, perpendicular to r
the moment arm r sin theta
mcqs.why: The component of F along r, F cos theta, pulls along the line joining the point to the axis and produces no turning; only the perpendicular component F sin theta turns the body.

mcqs.q: Two equal and opposite parallel forces of 10 N each are applied at two different points of a body (a couple). The resultant force and resultant torque are:
options: resultant force 20 N, resultant torque zero
resultant force zero, resultant torque zero
resultant force 20 N, resultant torque non-zero
resultant force zero, resultant torque non-zero
mcqs.why: The resultant force is 10 - 10 = 0, so the body does not translate; but the moments of the two forces about the centre act in the same rotational sense and add up, giving a non-zero resultant torque that rotates the body.

mcqs.q: The centre of gravity of a body is the point:
options: at which the whole weight of the body acts
where the body's volume is concentrated
which always lies outside the body
where the body's density is greatest
mcqs.why: The centre of gravity is the point, inside or outside the body, at which the whole weight of the body acts, i.e. through which the resultant of the gravitational pull on all its particles passes; near the Earth's surface it coincides with the centre of mass.

mcqs.q: A cone resting on its wide circular base is in stable equilibrium because a slight tilt:
options: lowers its centre of gravity and it rolls away
neither raises nor lowers its centre of gravity
raises its centre of gravity and it returns to its original position
moves its centre of gravity outside its base
mcqs.why: The cone on its wide circular base is the chapter's example of stable equilibrium: a slight tilt raises its centre of gravity, so it returns to its original position when released.

mcqs.q: The two basic principles of stability applied in designing balancing toys and racing cars are:
options: keep the centre of gravity as high as possible and the base narrow
keep the centre of gravity as low as possible and make the base of support as wide as possible
make the body as light as possible and the base round
keep the weight on one side and the base small
mcqs.why: Stability requires (1) the centre of gravity kept as low as possible and (2) the base of support made as wide as possible, so the vertical line through the centre of gravity stays well inside the base even when the body is tilted; racing cars are built low and wide on exactly these principles.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4.1 A car travels at the same speed around two curves with different radii. For which radius the car experiences more centripetal force? Prove your answer.

From Fc = m v^2 / r, for the same car (same m) at the same speed v, the centripetal force is inversely proportional to the radius: Fc is proportional to 1/r. So the curve of smaller radius needs the larger centripetal force. Proof with numbers: halving r (with m and v fixed) gives Fc' = m v^2 / (r/2) = 2 m v^2 / r = 2 Fc, i.e. double the force. Hence friction must grip more strongly on the sharper curve.

Q: 4.2 A ripe mango does not normally fall from the tree. But when the branch of the tree is shaken, the mango falls down easily. Can you tell the reason?

The stalk holds the mango against small disturbances because of the grip of the stem and static effects; the mango's own inertia resists ordinary movements. When the branch is shaken sharply, the branch moves suddenly but the heavy mango tends to stay where it was (inertia of rest). This sudden relative jerk strains the stalk beyond its strength and snaps it, so the mango falls.

Q: 4.3 Discuss the concepts of stability and centre of gravity in relation to objects toppling over. Provide an example where an object's centre of gravity affects its stability, and explain how altering its base of support can influence stability.

An object topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support; then the weight itself produces a moment about the edge that overturns it. The lower the centre of gravity and the wider the base, the more the object can tilt before this happens, so it is more stable. Example: a double-decker bus remains stable in a turn while its centre of gravity stays over its wheel base, but a top-heavy loaded truck, whose centre of gravity is high, topples on the same turn; similarly a Bunsen burner or a table lamp is given a wide heavy base so that its centre of gravity stays within the base.

Q: 4.4 Why an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium?

Equilibrium requires zero acceleration: the resultant force on the body must be zero (first condition) and the resultant torque must also be zero (second condition). An accelerated body by definition has a changing velocity, which means a non-zero resultant force is acting on it, so the first condition fails and it cannot be in equilibrium.

Q: 4.5 Two boxes of the same weight but different heights are lying on the floor of a truck. If the truck makes a sudden stop, which box is more likely to tumble over? Why?

The taller box. Both boxes have the same weight, but the taller box has its centre of gravity higher up. When the truck stops suddenly, inertia makes the boxes lurch forward; the taller box's line of action of weight passes outside its base with a much smaller tilt, so its own weight then overturns it. The shorter, low-centre-of-gravity box stays upright.

mcqs.q: A car travels at the same speed around two curves of different radii. On which curve does it experience the greater centripetal force?
options: On the curve of larger radius
The force is the same on both curves
On the curve of smaller radius
It depends only on the mass of the car
mcqs.why: From Fc = m v^2 / r, for the same car (same m) at the same speed v, the centripetal force is inversely proportional to the radius, Fc proportional to 1/r, so the curve of smaller radius needs the larger centripetal force.

mcqs.q: For a car at fixed mass and speed, if the radius of the curve is halved, the centripetal force becomes:
mcqs.why: Halving r with m and v fixed gives Fc' = m v^2 / (r/2) = 2 m v^2 / r = 2 Fc, i.e. double the force, which is why friction must grip more strongly on the sharper curve.

mcqs.q: A ripe mango falls easily when the branch is shaken sharply, mainly because of:
options: the mango's inertia of rest: the branch moves suddenly but the heavy mango tends to stay where it was
the weight of the mango suddenly increases
the stalk becomes stronger when shaken
the centripetal force on the mango becomes zero
mcqs.why: When the branch is shaken sharply it moves suddenly, but the heavy mango tends to stay where it was due to inertia of rest; this sudden relative jerk strains the stalk beyond its strength and snaps it, so the mango falls.

mcqs.q: An object topples over when:
options: its centre of gravity is lowered
the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support
its base of support is widened
the clockwise and anticlockwise moments become equal
mcqs.why: An object topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support; then the weight itself produces a moment about the edge that overturns it.

mcqs.q: Why is a top-heavy loaded truck more likely to topple on a turn than a double-decker bus whose centre of gravity stays over its wheel base?
options: The truck is heavier, so its moments cancel
The bus has a wider base of support only
The truck's centre of gravity is high, so a smaller tilt moves its line of action of weight outside the base
The truck experiences no centripetal force
mcqs.why: The lower the centre of gravity and the wider the base, the more an object can tilt before the line of action of its weight passes outside the base. The top-heavy truck has a high centre of gravity, so it topples on the turn, while the bus remains stable while its centre of gravity stays over its wheel base.

mcqs.q: Why can an accelerated body not be in equilibrium?
options: Because its resultant torque is always zero
Because acceleration means a non-zero resultant force acts on it, so the first condition of equilibrium fails
Because it has no centre of gravity
mcqs.why: Equilibrium requires zero acceleration: the resultant force must be zero (first condition) and the resultant torque must be zero (second condition). An accelerated body has a changing velocity, which means a non-zero resultant force acts on it, so the first condition fails.

mcqs.q: Two boxes of the same weight but different heights lie on the floor of a truck. If the truck stops suddenly, which box is more likely to tumble over?
options: The shorter box, because its centre of gravity is lower
Both boxes are equally likely to tumble
Neither box can tumble because their weights are equal
The taller box, because its centre of gravity is higher
mcqs.why: Both boxes have the same weight, but the taller box has its centre of gravity higher up. When the truck stops suddenly, inertia makes the boxes lurch forward; the taller box's line of action of weight passes outside its base with a much smaller tilt, so its own weight overturns it.

mcqs.q: When the truck stops suddenly, the boxes lurch forward because of:
options: the couple formed by the wheels
mcqs.why: Inertia makes the boxes tend to keep moving forward when the truck stops suddenly; the taller box then topples because its high centre of gravity moves outside its base with only a small tilt, while the shorter, low-centre-of-gravity box stays upright.

mcqs.q: A Bunsen burner and a table lamp are given wide heavy bases so that:
options: their centre of gravity rises when tilted
their weight acts outside the base
their centre of gravity stays within the base, keeping them stable
mcqs.why: A wide heavy base keeps the vertical line through the centre of gravity within the base of support even when the object is tilted, so the weight produces no overturning moment and the object stays stable; the lower centre of gravity and wider base both increase stability.

mcqs.q: For a moving car on two curves at the same speed, the sharper (smaller radius) curve demands more from the tyres because:
options: the speed must increase on the sharper curve
friction must provide a larger centripetal force there
the mass of the car increases there
the centripetal force acts along the velocity there
mcqs.why: Since Fc = m v^2 / r is inversely proportional to r at fixed m and v, the smaller-radius curve needs the larger centripetal force, and that force is supplied by friction, so friction must grip more strongly on the sharper curve.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4.1 Explain the principle of moments with an example.

Principle of moments: when a body is in rotational equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point is equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point. Example: a see-saw balances when a 30 kg child sits 2 m from the pivot on one side and a 40 kg child sits 1.5 m on the other side: clockwise moment = 40 x 1.5 = 60 units and anticlockwise moment = 30 x 2 = 60 units (using mass x distance; with weights the moments are 600 N m each side). The moments are equal, so the see-saw stays balanced.

Q: 4.2 Describe how could you determine the centre of gravity of an irregular shaped lamina experimentally.

Make three small holes near the edges of the lamina. Suspend the lamina freely from a pin through the first hole and hang a plumb line from the same pin; mark the line of the string on the lamina. Repeat the suspension from the second and third holes, marking the plumb line each time. The three lines cross at a single point; that point is the centre of gravity of the lamina, because the weight acts along the plumb line in each free suspension.

Q: 4.3 State and explain two conditions of equilibrium.

First condition (translational equilibrium): the vector sum of all the external forces acting on the body must be zero, sum F = 0; the body then has no linear acceleration. Second condition (rotational equilibrium): the vector sum of all the torques acting on the body about any axis must be zero, sum torque = 0; equivalently, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments. A body satisfying both conditions is completely in equilibrium.

Q: 4.4 How the stability of an object can be improved? Give a few examples to support your answer.

Stability is improved by (1) lowering the centre of gravity and (2) widening the base of support. Examples: racing cars are made low and wide so they do not overturn on fast curves; ships load heavy cargo in the bottom (ballast) to keep the centre of gravity low; a table lamp and a Bunsen burner have wide heavy bases; a tight-rope walker carries a long pole which lowers and helps control the combined centre of gravity; double-decker buses carry passengers' heavy luggage in the lower compartment.

mcqs.q: According to the principle of moments, when a body is in rotational equilibrium:
options: the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point
all clockwise moments are zero and anticlockwise moments are not
the moments depend on the mass of the body only
mcqs.why: The principle of moments states that when a body is in rotational equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point is equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point.

mcqs.q: A see-saw balances with a 30 kg child 2 m from the pivot on one side and a 40 kg child 1.5 m on the other side. Using weights (g = 10 m/s^2), the moment on each side is:
options: 300 N m on one side and 400 N m on the other
mcqs.why: Weights: 30 x 10 = 300 N and 40 x 10 = 400 N. Moments: 300 x 2 = 600 N m and 400 x 1.5 = 600 N m. The clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal, so by the principle of moments the see-saw stays balanced.

mcqs.q: To find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina experimentally, the lamina is suspended freely from a pin through a hole near its edge and:
options: its mass is measured with a balance
a plumb line is hung from the same pin and the line of the string is marked on the lamina
it is floated on water and its level is marked
it is cut into two equal halves
mcqs.why: Suspend the lamina freely from a pin through a hole near its edge and hang a plumb line from the same pin; mark the line of the string on the lamina, then repeat from other holes. The marked lines cross at the centre of gravity.

mcqs.q: In the lamina experiment, the lines marked from three different suspension points all cross at one point, which is the centre of gravity, because:
options: the lamina has the same thickness everywhere
the holes are near the edges of the lamina
the centre of gravity is always at the geometric centre
the weight acts along the plumb line in each free suspension
mcqs.why: In each free suspension the lamina hangs so that its weight acts along the plumb line; marking that line for three different holes gives three lines through the point where the whole weight acts, and they cross at the centre of gravity of the lamina.

mcqs.q: The first condition of equilibrium (translational equilibrium) requires that:
options: the vector sum of all external forces on the body is zero, sum F = 0
the sum of all torques is non-zero
the body must be at rest
the clockwise moments equal the mass of the body
mcqs.why: The first condition of equilibrium is that the vector sum of all the external forces acting on the body must be zero, sum F = 0; the body then has no linear acceleration.

mcqs.q: The second condition of equilibrium (rotational equilibrium) requires that:
options: the sum of clockwise moments is greater than the sum of anticlockwise moments
the vector sum of all torques about any axis is zero, sum torque = 0
the resultant force is zero but torques may be non-zero
the body must rotate at constant speed
mcqs.why: The second condition is that the vector sum of all the torques acting on the body about any axis must be zero, sum torque = 0; equivalently, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.

mcqs.q: A body is completely in equilibrium when:
options: only the first condition, sum F = 0, is satisfied
only the second condition, sum torque = 0, is satisfied
it is completely at rest and cannot move
both conditions are satisfied: sum F = 0 and sum torque = 0
mcqs.why: A body satisfying both conditions, sum F = 0 (translational) and sum torque = 0 (rotational), is completely in equilibrium, with no linear and no angular acceleration.

mcqs.q: Ships load heavy cargo in the bottom (ballast) in order to:
options: raise the centre of gravity of the ship
keep the centre of gravity low and so improve stability
narrow the base of support of the ship
increase the resultant torque on the ship
mcqs.why: Stability is improved by lowering the centre of gravity and widening the base of support. Loading heavy cargo low in the ship (ballast) keeps the combined centre of gravity low, so the ship does not overturn easily.

mcqs.q: Racing cars are made low and wide so that they:
options: have a higher centre of gravity on fast curves
do not overturn on fast curves
keep their centre of gravity outside the wheel base
mcqs.why: Lowering the centre of gravity and widening the base of support both improve stability; racing cars are made low and wide on exactly these principles so that they do not overturn on fast curves.

mcqs.q: A tight-rope walker carries a long pole mainly because it:
options: increases the walker's weight so moments increase
raises the combined centre of gravity
applies the law of conservation of momentum
lowers and helps control the combined centre of gravity
mcqs.why: Stability is improved by lowering the centre of gravity. The tight-rope walker's long pole lowers and helps control the combined centre of gravity of walker plus pole, helping him stay balanced, just as the bamboo stick example applies the principle of moments.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4.1 A force of 200 N is acting on a cart at an angle of 30 degrees with the horizontal direction. Find the x and y-components of the force.

Given: force F = 200 N; angle theta = 30 degrees with the horizontal. Step 1: Formula: Fx = F cos theta. Step 2: Fx = 200 x cos 30 = 200 x 0.866 = 173.2 N. Step 3: Formula: Fy = F sin theta. Step 4: Fy = 200 x sin 30 = 200 x 0.5 = 100 N. Final answer: x-component = 173.2 N; y-component = 100 N.

Q: 4.2 A force of 300 N is applied perpendicularly at the knob of a door to open it as shown in the given figure. If the knob is 1.2 m away from the hinge, what is the torque applied? Is it positive or negative torque?

Given: force F = 300 N applied perpendicularly; moment arm r = 1.2 m. Step 1: Formula: torque = F x r (force perpendicular to the arm). Step 2: Torque = 300 x 1.2 = 360 N m. Step 3: The force turns the door in the opening (anticlockwise, as seen in the figure) sense, which is taken as positive. Final answer: torque = 360 N m, positive.

Q: 4.3 Two weights are hanging from a metre rule at the positions as shown in the given figure (w at 40 cm on one side of the centre of gravity, 4 N at 30 cm on the other side). If the metre rule is balanced at its centre of gravity (C.G), find the unknown weight w.

Given (from the figure): unknown weight w hangs 40 cm to the left of the centre of gravity (the pivot); a 4 N weight hangs 30 cm to the right; the rule balances. Step 1: Principle of moments: anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment about the pivot. Step 2: w x 40 cm = 4 N x 30 cm. Step 3: w = (4 x 30) / 40 = 120 / 40 = 3 N. Final answer: unknown weight w = 3 N.

Q: 4.4 A see-saw is balanced with two children sitting near either end. Child A weighs 30 kg and sits 2 metres away from the pivot, while child B weighs 40 kg and sits 1.5 metres from the pivot. Calculate the total moment on each side and determine if the see-saw is in equilibrium.

Given: child A mass 30 kg at 2 m from the pivot; child B mass 40 kg at 1.5 m. Step 1: Weights: A = 30 x 10 = 300 N; B = 40 x 10 = 400 N. Step 2: Moment of A about the pivot = 300 x 2 = 600 N m. Step 3: Moment of B about the pivot = 400 x 1.5 = 600 N m. Step 4: The moments on the two sides are equal and opposite in sense, so their sum is zero. Final answer: the see-saw is in equilibrium. (Note: the book prints the value 60, which is the mass x distance product on each side, 30 x 2 = 40 x 1.5; with weights the moments are 600 N m each side and the conclusion is the same.)

Q: 4.5 A crowbar is used to lift a box as shown in the given figure. If the downward force of 250 N is applied at the end of the bar, how much weight does the other end bear? The crowbar itself has negligible weight. (From the figure, the box is 5 cm from the fulcrum and the force acts 30 cm from the fulcrum.)

Given (from the figure): the box rests 5 cm from the fulcrum; the 250 N downward force is applied 30 cm from the fulcrum on the other side; weight of crowbar negligible. Step 1: Principle of moments about the fulcrum: W x 5 cm = F x 30 cm. Step 2: W = (250 x 30) / 5 = 7500 / 5 = 1500 N. Final answer: the other end bears a weight of 1500 N.

Q: 4.6 A 30 cm long spanner is used to open the nut of a car. If the torque required for it is 150 N m, how much force F should be applied on the spanner as shown in the figure given below.

Given: length of spanner r = 30 cm = 0.30 m; torque required = 150 N m. Step 1: Formula: torque = F x r, so F = torque / r. Step 2: F = 150 / 0.30 = 500 N. Final answer: force to be applied = 500 N, perpendicular to the spanner at its end.

Q: 4.7 A 5 N ball hanging from a rope is pulled to the right by a horizontal force F. The rope makes an angle of 60 degrees with the ceiling, as shown in the given figure. Determine the magnitude of force F and tension T in the string.

Given: weight of ball W = 5 N; the rope makes 60 degrees with the ceiling, i.e. 30 degrees with the vertical; horizontal force F pulls the ball. Step 1: Resolve the tension T: vertical component T cos 30 balances the weight: T cos 30 = 5. Step 2: T = 5 / 0.866 = 5.8 N. Step 3: Horizontal component of tension balances F: F = T sin 30 = 5.8 x 0.5 = 2.9 N. Final answer: force F = 2.9 N; tension T = 5.8 N.

Q: 4.8 A signboard is suspended by means of two steel wires as shown in the given figure. If the weight of the board is 200 N, what is the tension in the strings? (From the figure, the wires are attached symmetrically, 2 m on each side of the centre of the board.)

Given: weight of board = 200 N acting at its centre; the two wires are attached symmetrically, 2 m on each side of the centre (from the figure). Step 1: Vertical equilibrium: T1 + T2 = 200 N. Step 2: Moments about the centre: T1 x 2 = T2 x 2, so T1 = T2. Step 3: 2 T1 = 200, so T1 = 100 N and T2 = 100 N. Final answer: tension in each string = 100 N.

Q: 4.9 One girl of 30 kg mass sits 1.6 m from the axis of a see-saw. Another girl of mass 40 kg wants to sit on the other side, so that the see-saw may remain in equilibrium. How far away from the axis, the other girl may sit?

Given: girl 1 mass 30 kg at 1.6 m from the axis; girl 2 mass 40 kg at unknown distance d on the other side. Step 1: Principle of moments for equilibrium: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. Step 2: 40 x d = 30 x 1.6 (using masses, since g is common). Step 3: d = 48 / 40 = 1.2 m. Final answer: the other girl should sit 1.2 m from the axis.

Q: 4.10 Find the tension in each string as shown in the given figure, if the block weighs 150 N. (From the figure, the block hangs from a junction held by one horizontal string and one string at 60 degrees to the horizontal.)

Given: block weight = 150 N hanging from the junction of two strings; from the figure, one string is horizontal and the other makes 60 degrees with the horizontal. Step 1: Vertical equilibrium: the vertical component of the slanted string's tension balances the weight: T1 sin 60 = 150. Step 2: T1 = 150 / 0.866 = 173.2 N. Step 3: Horizontal equilibrium: T2 = T1 cos 60 = 173.2 x 0.5 = 86.6 N. Final answer: tension in the slanted string = 173.2 N; tension in the horizontal string = 86.6 N.

mcqs.q: A force of 200 N acts on a cart at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Its x-component is:
mcqs.why: Given: F = 200 N, theta = 30 degrees. Formula: Fx = F cos theta. Substitution: Fx = 200 x cos 30 = 200 x 0.866 = 173.2 N. Result: x-component = 173.2 N (the y-component is Fy = 200 x sin 30 = 100 N).

mcqs.q: A force of 300 N is applied perpendicularly at the knob of a door, 1.2 m from the hinge. The torque applied is:
mcqs.why: Given: F = 300 N applied perpendicularly, moment arm r = 1.2 m. Formula: torque = F x r. Substitution: torque = 300 x 1.2 = 360 N m. Result: torque = 360 N m, positive, because the force turns the door in the opening (anticlockwise) sense.

mcqs.q: A metre rule balances at its centre of gravity with an unknown weight w hanging 40 cm to the left of the pivot and a 4 N weight 30 cm to the right. The unknown weight w is:
mcqs.why: Given: w at 40 cm on one side, 4 N at 30 cm on the other side, rule balanced at its centre of gravity. Formula (principle of moments): anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment, so w x 40 cm = 4 N x 30 cm. Substitution: w = (4 x 30) / 40 = 120 / 40 = 3. Result: w = 3 N.

mcqs.q: On a balanced see-saw, child A of mass 30 kg sits 2 m from the pivot and child B of mass 40 kg sits 1.5 m from the pivot. The moment on each side (g = 10 m/s^2) is:
options: 600 N m on each side, so the see-saw is in equilibrium
600 N m on one side and 60 N m on the other
mcqs.why: Given: A: mass 30 kg at 2 m; B: mass 40 kg at 1.5 m; g = 10 m/s^2. Weights: A = 30 x 10 = 300 N, B = 40 x 10 = 400 N. Formula: moment = weight x distance. Substitution: A: 300 x 2 = 600 N m; B: 400 x 1.5 = 600 N m. Result: 600 N m on each side, equal and opposite in sense, so the see-saw is in equilibrium. Note: the book prints 60, which is only the mass x distance product (30 x 2 = 40 x 1.5 = 60); that is a misprint for the moment, because with weights the true moments are 600 N m on each side.

mcqs.q: A crowbar lifts a box resting 5 cm from the fulcrum when a downward force of 250 N is applied 30 cm from the fulcrum on the other side. The weight borne by the other end is:
mcqs.why: Given: box 5 cm from the fulcrum, applied force F = 250 N at 30 cm from the fulcrum, crowbar weight negligible. Formula (principle of moments about the fulcrum): W x 5 cm = F x 30 cm. Substitution: W = (250 x 30) / 5 = 7500 / 5 = 1500. Result: the other end bears a weight of 1500 N.

mcqs.q: A 30 cm long spanner must produce a torque of 150 N m to open a nut. The force that should be applied perpendicularly at its end is:
mcqs.why: Given: length of spanner r = 30 cm = 0.30 m, torque required = 150 N m. Formula: torque = F x r, so F = torque / r. Substitution: F = 150 / 0.30 = 500. Result: force to be applied = 500 N, perpendicular to the spanner at its end.

mcqs.q: A 5 N ball hangs from a rope making 60 degrees with the ceiling (30 degrees with the vertical) and is pulled by a horizontal force F. The tension T in the rope and the force F are:
mcqs.why: Given: weight W = 5 N, rope at 30 degrees to the vertical. Method: resolve the tension. Vertical equilibrium: T cos 30 = 5, so T = 5 / 0.866 = 5.8 N. Horizontal equilibrium: F = T sin 30 = 5.8 x 0.5 = 2.9 N. Result: tension T = 5.8 N and horizontal force F = 2.9 N.

mcqs.q: A signboard of weight 200 N is suspended by two steel wires attached symmetrically, 2 m on each side of its centre. The tension in each wire is:
mcqs.why: Given: weight of board = 200 N acting at its centre, wires attached symmetrically 2 m on each side of the centre. Vertical equilibrium: T1 + T2 = 200 N. Moments about the centre: T1 x 2 = T2 x 2, so T1 = T2. Substitution: 2 T1 = 200, so T1 = 100 N. Result: tension in each string = 100 N.

mcqs.q: A girl of mass 30 kg sits 1.6 m from the axis of a see-saw. How far from the axis should a girl of mass 40 kg sit on the other side for equilibrium?
mcqs.why: Given: girl 1 mass 30 kg at 1.6 m; girl 2 mass 40 kg at unknown distance d. Formula (principle of moments): clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment; using masses since g is common: 40 x d = 30 x 1.6. Substitution: d = 48 / 40 = 1.2. Result: the other girl should sit 1.2 m from the axis.

mcqs.q: A block of weight 150 N hangs from a junction held by one horizontal string and one string at 60 degrees to the horizontal. The tension in the slanted string is:
mcqs.why: Given: block weight = 150 N, one string horizontal, the other at 60 degrees to the horizontal. Method: vertical equilibrium, the vertical component of the slanted string's tension T1 balances the weight: T1 sin 60 = 150. Substitution: T1 = 150 / 0.866 = 173.2 N. Result: tension in the slanted string = 173.2 N (and the horizontal string's tension is T2 = T1 cos 60 = 173.2 x 0.5 = 86.6 N).

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5.1 What is the work done on an object that remains at rest when a force is applied on it?

Zero. Work is done only when the point of application of the force moves: W = F d cos theta. The object remains at rest, so its displacement d is zero and the work done is zero, however large the force may be.

Q: 5.2 A slow-moving car may have more kinetic energy than a fast-moving motorcycle. How is this possible?

Kinetic energy depends on mass as well as speed: K.E. = (1/2) m v^2. A car has a much larger mass than a motorcycle. Even at a smaller speed, its large mass can more than compensate, e.g. a 1200 kg car at 10 m/s has K.E. = 60,000 J, while a 150 kg motorcycle at 20 m/s has K.E. = 30,000 J.

Q: 5.3 A force F1 does 5 J of work in 10 s. Another force F2 does 3 J of work in 5 s. Which force delivers greater power?

Power is work divided by time. P1 = 5 J / 10 s = 0.5 W. P2 = 3 J / 5 s = 0.6 W. So F2 delivers the greater power, although it does less total work, because it does its work in a much shorter time.

Q: 5.4 A woman runs up a flight of stairs. The gain in her gravitational potential energy is 4500 J. If she runs up the same stairs with twice the speed, what will be her gain in potential energy?

Still 4500 J. The gain in gravitational potential energy is mgh; it depends on her mass and the height of the stairs only, not on the speed of climbing. Running twice as fast only doubles the power she develops, not the energy gained.

Q: 5.5 Define work and its SI unit.

Work is done when a force acts on a body and moves it in the direction of the force; quantitatively, work = force x distance moved in the direction of the force (W = F d, or F d cos theta for an angled force). Its SI unit is the joule (J): one joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves a body through one metre in its own direction.

Q: 5.6 What is the potential energy of a body of mass m when it is raised through a height h?

Potential energy = m g h, where m is the mass, g the acceleration due to gravity and h the height raised. This is exactly the work done against gravity in lifting the body through h, and it is stored in the body as gravitational potential energy.

Q: 5.7 Find an expression for the kinetic energy of a moving body.

Let a body of mass m start from rest and be pushed by a constant force F through a distance S, reaching velocity v. Step 1: Work done W = F S. Step 2: From F = m a and 2aS = v^2 - 0, we get S = v^2 / 2a, so W = m a x v^2 / 2a = (1/2) m v^2. Step 3: This work is stored as the energy of motion, so kinetic energy K.E. = (1/2) m v^2.

Q: 5.8 Define efficiency of a working system. Why a system cannot have 100% efficiency?

Efficiency is the ratio of the useful output energy to the total input energy of a working system, often expressed as a percentage: efficiency = (useful output / total input) x 100. No system can reach 100 percent, because part of the input energy is always wasted against friction and is converted into heat, sound and wear in the moving parts.

Q: 5.9 What is power? Define the unit used for it.

Power is the rate of doing work, i.e. the work done per unit time: P = W / t. Its unit is the watt (W): one watt is the power of a system that does one joule of work in one second (1 W = 1 J/s). Larger units are the kilowatt (10^3 W) and megawatt (10^6 W).

Q: 5.10 Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable energy sources.

Renewable sources are replaced by nature in a short time and cannot be used up: solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal and biomass energy. Non-renewable sources took millions of years to form and are finished once used: coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels) and nuclear fuels. Renewable sources are also mostly pollution-free, while burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and smoke.

lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5.1 Can the kinetic energy of a body ever be negative?

No. Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2. Mass is always positive and v appears squared, so the product is never negative; at rest it is zero. Direction does not matter because speed squared is used.

Q: 5.2 Which one has the greater kinetic energy; an object travelling with a velocity v or an object twice as heavy travelling with a velocity of (1/2) v?

First object: K.E.1 = (1/2) m v^2. Second object: mass 2m, velocity v/2, so K.E.2 = (1/2) (2m) (v/2)^2 = (1/2) (2m) (v^2/4) = (1/4) m v^2 = (1/2) K.E.1. So the first object (mass m at velocity v) has the greater kinetic energy, twice as much. Velocity matters more than mass because it is squared.

Q: 5.3 A car is moving along a curved road at constant speed. Does its kinetic energy change?

No, its kinetic energy does not change. Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed only: K.E. = (1/2) m v^2. On the curve only the direction of motion changes; the speed stays constant, so the kinetic energy remains the same (though the velocity and momentum, being vectors, do change).

Q: 5.4 Comment on the statement. "An object has one joule of potential energy."

The statement is incomplete. Potential energy has no absolute value: it is measured relative to a chosen reference level (e.g. the ground or a table top) where it is taken as zero. The object has one joule of potential energy with respect to some stated level, meaning one joule of work was done against gravity (or can be recovered) relative to that level. The reference level must always be understood or stated.

Q: 5.5 While driving on a motorway, tyre of a vehicle sometimes bursts. What may be its cause?

At high motorway speeds friction between the tyres and the road heats the air inside the tyre strongly. The heated air expands and its pressure rises; a worn or weak tyre wall cannot bear the extra pressure and bursts. Under-inflated tyres flex more, heat even faster, and burst sooner.

Q: 5.6 While playing cricket on a street, the ball smashes a window pane. Describe the energy changes in this event.

The moving ball has kinetic energy (from the chemical energy of the batsman's muscles). On hitting the pane, this kinetic energy does work breaking the bonds of the glass: part changes into the kinetic energy of the flying glass pieces, part into sound energy of the crash, and part into heat. The ball itself slows down, losing kinetic energy in the process.

Q: 5.7 A man rowing boat upstream is at rest with respect to the shore. Is he doing work?

In the physics sense, no work is done on the boat: the boat does not move relative to the shore, so there is no displacement and W = F x 0 = 0. The man certainly spends energy: his muscles do work against the flowing water to hold the boat in place, and that energy is wasted as heat and in moving water, but no work is done on the boat itself.

Q: 5.8 A cyclist goes downhill from the top of a steep hill without pedalling and takes it to the top of the next hill. (i) Draw a diagram of what happened. (ii) Analyse this event in terms of potential and kinetic energy. Label your diagram using these terms.

(i) Diagram (to be drawn in the notes): draw two hills side by side; mark the start at the top of the first hill as maximum potential energy, the valley bottom as maximum kinetic energy, and the top of the second (lower) hill as potential energy again. (ii) Analysis: at the top of the first hill the cyclist has maximum gravitational potential energy and almost no kinetic energy. Rolling down, potential energy converts into kinetic energy, so speed is greatest at the bottom. Climbing the next hill, kinetic energy converts back into potential energy. Because of friction and air resistance, some energy is lost as heat, so he reaches a lower height on the second hill than his starting height.

Q: 5.9 Is timber or wood renewable source of heat energy? Comment.

Wood is renewable only if it is used at the rate at which trees regrow. Trees absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, and burning wood releases roughly the same amount, so managed wood is nearly carbon-neutral. But if forests are cut faster than they regrow, wood becomes effectively non-renewable and also destroys habitats; and burning it in open fires is inefficient and produces smoke. So timber is a renewable source of heat only under sustainable replanting.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5.1 What is meant by kinetic energy? State its unit. Describe how it is determined.

Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body by virtue of its motion. Its unit is the joule (J). It is determined by the work needed to bring the body from rest to its present speed: a force F acting through distance S on mass m gives W = F S = m a x v^2 / 2a, so K.E. = (1/2) m v^2. It therefore depends on the mass of the body and on the square of its speed.

Q: 5.2 State the law of conservation of energy. Explain it with the help of an example of a body falling from certain height in terms of its potential energy and kinetic energy.

Law: energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another, and the total energy of an isolated system remains constant. Example: a body of mass m at height h has potential energy mgh and no kinetic energy. As it falls, height and potential energy decrease while speed and kinetic energy increase; at every point mgh + (1/2) m v^2 stays constant (neglecting air resistance). Just before striking the ground all the energy is kinetic: (1/2) m v^2 = mgh, giving v = sqrt(2gh).

Q: 5.3 Differentiate between renewable and non renewable sources of energy. Give three examples for each.

Renewable sources are naturally replenished in a short time and will not run out: examples are solar energy, wind energy and hydroelectric energy (also biomass and geothermal). Non-renewable sources exist in fixed amounts, took millions of years to form and are exhausted by use: examples are coal, petroleum (oil) and natural gas (also nuclear fuel). Burning non-renewable fossil fuels also produces pollution and carbon dioxide, which most renewable sources avoid.

Q: 5.4 Explain what is meant by efficiency of a machine. How is it calculated? Why there is a limit for the efficiency of a machine?

The efficiency of a machine is the ratio of its useful output energy (or power) to the total input energy (or power): efficiency = useful output / total input, expressed as a percentage by multiplying by 100. There is always a limit below 100 percent because part of the input is unavoidably wasted: friction between moving parts converts energy into heat and sound, and no machine can be made completely frictionless.

Q: 5.5 Describe the process of electricity generation by drawing a block diagram of the process in the following cases. (i) Hydroelectric power generations (ii) Fossil fuels

(i) Hydroelectric generation (block diagram in words): potential energy of water stored in a dam - kinetic energy of falling water - kinetic energy of the turbine - electrical energy from the generator - transmission to homes. (ii) Fossil fuels: chemical energy of coal/oil/gas - heat energy released by burning - kinetic energy of steam - kinetic energy of the turbine - electrical energy from the generator. In both cases a turbine spins a generator; only the source that drives the turbine differs. (Draw the two chains as labelled block diagrams in the notes.)

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body by virtue of its:
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body by virtue of its motion. It is determined by the work needed to bring the body from rest to its present speed, giving K.E. = (1/2) m v^2.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of kinetic energy?
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy is a form of energy and work, so its unit is the joule (J), the same unit as work: one joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves a body through one metre.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy is determined by the work needed to bring a body from rest to its present speed, which gives:
options: K.E. = F d cos theta only
mcqs.why: A force F acting through distance S on mass m gives W = F S = m a x v^2 / 2a, so K.E. = (1/2) m v^2. It therefore depends on the mass of the body and on the square of its speed.

mcqs.q: The law of conservation of energy states that:
options: Energy can be created but not destroyed
Energy can be destroyed but not created
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another and the total energy remains constant
The total energy of a system always decreases
mcqs.why: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another, and the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

mcqs.q: A body falls freely from a height (neglecting air resistance). At every point during the fall, mgh + (1/2) m v^2:
options: Decreases to zero at the ground
Is zero at the top of the fall
mcqs.why: As the body falls, height and potential energy decrease while speed and kinetic energy increase; at every point mgh + (1/2) m v^2 stays constant. Just before striking the ground all the energy is kinetic: (1/2) m v^2 = mgh, giving v = sqrt(2 g h).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
mcqs.why: Renewable sources are naturally replenished in a short time and will not run out: solar energy, wind energy and hydroelectric energy (also biomass and geothermal). Coal, petroleum and natural gas are non-renewable.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-renewable source of energy?
mcqs.why: Non-renewable sources exist in fixed amounts, took millions of years to form and are exhausted by use: coal, petroleum (oil) and natural gas (also nuclear fuel). Burning them also produces pollution and carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: The efficiency of a machine is calculated as:
options: Total input divided by useful output
Useful output divided by total input, multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage
mcqs.why: The efficiency of a machine is the ratio of its useful output energy (or power) to the total input energy (or power): efficiency = useful output / total input, expressed as a percentage by multiplying by 100.

mcqs.q: Why is there always a limit below 100 percent for the efficiency of a machine?
options: Because every machine is already 100 percent efficient
Because friction between moving parts converts part of the input energy into heat and sound, and no machine can be made completely frictionless
Because efficiency is limited by the size of the watt
Because output energy can exceed input energy
mcqs.why: Part of the input is unavoidably wasted: friction between moving parts converts energy into heat and sound, and no machine can be made completely frictionless, so efficiency always stays below 100 percent.

mcqs.q: In both hydroelectric generation and fossil-fuel generation, electricity is finally produced by:
mcqs.why: Hydroelectric: potential energy of dam water - kinetic energy of falling water - kinetic energy of the turbine - electrical energy from the generator. Fossil fuels: chemical energy - heat from burning - kinetic energy of steam - kinetic energy of the turbine - electrical energy. In both cases a turbine spins a generator; only the source driving the turbine differs.
