lessons.notes_html:
Q: 9.1 Is the theory of science an ultimate truth? Describe briefly.

No. A scientific theory is not an ultimate or final truth. The theories and laws of physics are human-made ideas about how things work; they stand only as long as experiments support them and are liable to be disproved or modified when new facts and insights appear. For example, Newton's picture of gravity was later refined by Einstein's theory of relativity.

Q: 9.2 Do you think that the existing laws of nature may need a change in future? Describe briefly.

Yes, possibly. Laws of nature are statements accepted because they have always agreed with observations so far. Future advances may bring fresh facts that the old law cannot explain, and then the law is modified or replaced by a more general one; for example, the laws of mechanics were extended at very high speeds by relativity and at atomic sizes by quantum theory. Science keeps its laws open to change on evidence.

Q: 9.3 Describe three jobs that need the use of scientific knowledge.

(1) A doctor uses the scientific knowledge of the body, germs and medicines to diagnose and treat disease. (2) A civil engineer uses the laws of mechanics and the properties of materials to design safe bridges and buildings. (3) A software engineer uses logic, mathematics and the science of computation to build useful applications. (Other valid examples: an agricultural scientist improving crops, a pharmacist preparing medicines, a meteorologist forecasting weather.)

Q: 9.4 Describe when a theory is rejected or needs its modification.

A theory is rejected or modified when careful, repeated experiments disagree with its predictions and the disagreement cannot be removed by correcting the experiment. If only part of the theory fails, it is modified; if its basic claim is contradicted by reliable evidence, the theory is rejected and a new hypothesis is built and tested in its place.

Q: 9.5 Comment on the statement. "A theory capable of being proved right but not being proved wrong is not a scientific theory".

The statement expresses the principle of falsifiability. A scientific theory must make testable predictions that could, in principle, turn out to be wrong. A claim that can be 'proved right' but can never be proved wrong, whatever happens, makes no definite prediction and cannot be tested; such a claim is not a scientific theory but a belief.

Q: 9.6 What has been the general reaction to new ideas about established truths?

New ideas that challenge established truths have generally met with resistance at first: ridicule, opposition and even persecution (as happened with the heliocentric theory in its time). Scientists and society accept a new idea only slowly, as experimental evidence in its favour accumulates; once verified repeatedly, the new idea itself becomes the established truth. This caution is part of the scientific method, but it also shows that established truth is never beyond question.

Q: 9.7 If a hypothesis is not testable, is the hypothesis wrong? Explain.

Not necessarily wrong, but not scientific either. A hypothesis that cannot be tested by observation or experiment can neither be proved nor disproved, so science can do nothing with it; it remains a speculation or belief. For a hypothesis to enter the scientific method it must lead to predictions that can be checked.

Q: 9.8 Explain how a small amount of data cannot prove that a prediction is always correct but can prove it is not always correct.

A prediction claims something will always happen in stated conditions. A few successful observations agree with it but cannot prove it for all the unobserved cases: the next trial might fail. But a single genuine failure is enough to prove the prediction is not always correct. So small amounts of confirming data give only weak support, while one clear contrary result can falsify the claim; that is why theories need testing many times, in many situations.

Q: 9.9 What is the relationship between an experiment and a hypothesis?

An experiment is the test of a hypothesis. The hypothesis proposes an explanation and predicts what should happen in a given situation; the experiment is designed to check that prediction under controlled conditions. If the results agree, the hypothesis is supported and may grow into a theory; if they disagree (lack of agreement), the hypothesis is changed or rejected, as shown in the scientific method flow chart.

Q: 9.10 Describe why the solution of complex problems need interdisciplinary research and collaboration.

Complex problems (climate change, a new disease, designing an aircraft) do not belong to one science: they involve physics, chemistry, biology, mathematics, computing and social factors at the same time. No single researcher masters all of these, so specialists must collaborate, each contributing the methods and knowledge of his or her field; the shared, interdisciplinary picture is what produces a workable solution.

Q: 9.1 What are the main branches of Physics? State briefly.

Mechanics: motion, forces and machines. Heat (thermal physics): temperature and the behaviour of heat. Optics: light, its propagation, reflection, refraction and optical instruments. Electromagnetism: electricity, magnetism and their applications. Acoustics: sound and its properties. Atomic and nuclear physics: the structure of the atom and the nucleus and their energy. (Also: solid state/electronics in modern physics.) Each branch studies one group of phenomena of matter and energy.

Q: 9.2 What is meant by interdisciplinary fields of Physics? Give three examples.

Interdisciplinary fields of physics are areas formed by the integration and interaction of physics with other disciplines, where the methods of physics are applied to the other field's problems. Examples: (1) Biophysics: physical methods applied to living organisms, e.g. imaging and biomechanics. (2) Astrophysics: physics of stars, planets and the universe. (3) Geophysics: physics applied to the Earth, e.g. earthquakes and the Earth's magnetic field. (Also climate physics and computational physics.)

Q: 9.3 What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.

The scientific method is the specific, systematic approach used to search for the truth about a natural phenomenon or event. Steps with the book's example of light: (1) Observation: shadows of objects are sharp and similar in shape to the objects. (2) Hypothesis: light travels in a straight line. (3) Experiment: light is passed through apertures and past obstacles; the bright regions and shadows agree with straight-line travel. (4) Theory: the verified assumption becomes the theory of rectilinear propagation of light, a logical explanation applicable to similar phenomena. (5) Prediction: the theory predicts that the shadow of a ball will be round and of a block rectangular. (6) Law: after the theory is tested many times and generally accepted, 'light travels in a straight line' stands as a law. Throughout, the theory must remain falsifiable.

Q: 9.4 Differentiate the terms, science, technology and engineering with examples.

Science is the collective knowledge about natural phenomena, gained by observation and experiment: e.g. the laws of thermodynamics. Technology is the methods and techniques developed by using scientific knowledge to make useful products: e.g. automobile technology built on thermodynamics, radar on the reflection of electromagnetic waves, laser devices on atomic physics. Engineering is the process of applying technologies and scientific principles to design and build things that meet specific needs, also weighing cost and safety: e.g. a civil engineer designs a bridge to withstand wind, earthquakes and traffic; a software engineer designs a user-friendly phone application; an aviation engineer chooses light, strong materials for an aircraft.

Q: 9.5 What is the scope of Physics in everyday life? Give some examples.

Physics is at work in almost everything we use. Examples: electricity and electronics run our lights, fans, phones and computers; mechanics and thermodynamics run our vehicles and refrigerators and air conditioners; optics gives us spectacles, cameras and microscopes; electromagnetism gives radio, television and radar; medical physics gives X-rays, ultrasound and laser treatment. The advancement of scientific knowledge through technology and engineering has changed the outlook of mankind and made life easier and more comfortable.
